div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPIIS. "How did Flimgilt get rich ?" "By his shrewd speculation." "And how did Fucash happen to lose his little property ?" "Oh, he went and dab- bled in stocks." MRS. GABLETON—" I understand that your hus- band cannot meet his creditors." Mrs. Fale—" On the contrary, he says he can't help meeting them. That the reason he goes out so seldom." AT MIDNIGHT.—First Cat: "Why SO sad to- night, Thomas 2" Second Cat: "I feel so lonely and neglected 1 I've been weeping and wailing for an hour, and nobody has thrown anything at me !" WHEELER—" Miss Yellowleaf, will you ride tan- dem with me for-----" Miss Yellowleaf—" Oh, Mr. Wheeler, this is so sudden; but you'll find ma be- hind the parlour door; speak to her." DOMESTIC / can always tell when a man is the head of his family." "How do you tell ?" "When the man is boss the first boy is put in trousers before he is a year and a half old." TOMMY (fervently) : " Miss Thomson—Bessie— may I call you Bessie ?" Miss Thomson—" Yes, I think you may, as--" Tommy: "Oh, thank you, Bes.3ie—thank you!" Miss Thomson—" It isn't my name." "I DON'T know which is worse," muttered young Blunderheels, at the swell reception, retreating to a corner and wiping his perspiring brow; "but I believe I would rather be run over by a train than to step on one." ETHEL "Isn't it strange that Flossie attracts such intellectual men ? " Maud: "Oh, no; she told me she always planned her gowns when they talk to her, and that gives her face that interested expression." Mr. CASEY: "I'm a-goin' to take little pat to the circus when it comes. They charge half- price for children don't they ? " Mr. O'Rourke: " Yes ; an', bedad, it's no more'n right they should. The children don't enjoy it half as much as the grown folks." Oa, SAY I—Editor : "The metre in this poem Is defective." Contributor: "I meant it to be. The poem is entitled The Charge of the Gas Company.'" DEPENDS ON THE POINT Or VIEW.—" What is interest?" "Interests is what a man pays you when he borrows your money." "What is usury? "Usury is what you have to pay a man when you borrow his money." THE PRUDENT COURSE.—" Updyke is an ex- ceedingly quick-witted chap." "So?" "Yes. For irstance, last night, at Jammer's party, he unfortunately stepped on Miss Quickfire's dress, and ripped in the neighbourhood of three miles of ruffle off it." "I see. He immediately mollified her by some exceedingly witty apology." "Not much 1 He immediately disappeared." - AND GOOD HOPS Too.—Kate: "Well, it's a mercy you left Wurzelshire and have come to spend a few days with Hs, CousinQoel I suppose down where you live the people ttnow nothing of concerts or even social hops ?" Cousin Joe: •"Aw ! My father ha' ten acres o' nowt else but hops, but I dunno about soCial hops. We call urn Kent hops." AN IGNORANT CAPTAIN.—Farmer OR board a steamer (suffering a good deal from the rolling of the vessel) to friend: "This eapt'n don't under- stand his business. Why don't he keep in the furrows ? "

RATHER INCONSISTENT. —Father—" Come, young man, get your coat off and come with me." Tommy—" You're not going to lick me, are you, dad ? " Father—" Certainly. Didn't I tell you this morning that I would settle with you for your bad behaviour ?" Tommy—" Yes, but I thought it was only a joke, like when you told the grocer you was going to settle with him." "YES, sir," said Jordan, "I've come to the con. elusion that I amount to something after all. There have been times when I was disposed to believe that I was a mere cipher in the world, but I can never have so small an opinion of myself again." "What has caused this sudden change in your estimation of yourself ?" " 1 have just been talking to a politician who wants my vote." "PROVIDENT IN PERIL."—A youth who wanted money wrote home as follows Father,—lf you don't send me a cheque I'll drown myself." He presently received the following reply "John,— Pull off your clothes before you jump. Your mother can cut 'em down to fit Jemmie." Mr. Dapper is one of that class of men who are scrupulously neat in their personal appearance, but who never fail to leave chaos behind them in the scene of their preparations. A neighbour recently called on Mrs. Dapper, and remarked: "One rarely sees a neater man than your husband; he always looks as if he had just come out of a band-box." "Very true," returned Mrs. Dapper; "but "—with a sigh—" you ought to see the band- box !"

Mn.. SHENTPERSEIENT (at hotel table, a summer resort) : "Mein cracious Isaac, you little vool. Vat for you ask for bret?" Little Isaac: "1 vant bret mit my meat, fadder." Mr. Shentpershent : " Shnst hear dat ! He vants bret ven bret sell for only fife cents a loaf, an' he gan't eat a kavarter off a loaf, an' I pay fife dollars a day at dis hotel. Here, Isaac' eat dis bottle off olives. Day cost von tollar a bottle." BAGLEY (sternly): " Aurelia, let this thing stop right here. M. De Twirliger—" Aurelia : "Oh, paw! Do you forbid Arthur the house?" Bagley: "He may come every night in the week if he pleases but he shall not bring his dog into my parlour. Last night its howlings kept me awake for an hour." Aurelia : "Why paw! that was Arthur singing a selection from Erminie.'" PROOF OF WEAKNESS. —lsaacs : "A young man named Green vas abblying for a bosition in mein shtore, and he gives you as reference. Do you know him, Stickenheimer ? " Stickenheimer : "Yes. He vas a good mans. He vas von of mein very pest gustomers for den years." Isaacs (in disgust): " Ach I He gets not der bosition 1 I embloy no man vot is a fool." COULDN'T MAKE IT PAY. —Political Farmer (despondently) "Somehow I don't seem to make farmin' pay. "Maybe you haven't tried the right way. "Yes, I've done ev'ything. I've tended nieetin's, and j'ned clubs, and voted for every candidate that said he knowed the way to help us along. But it don't seem to do no good, an' I must say I'm gettin' clean discouraged.' GRATITUDE.—CIerk at the Gas Office; "Well, I suppose you've come to complain about your as bill again, have you ?" Patient Citizen: "No, sir; I've come round to thank you people. Some- body left a jet on in my daughter's bed-room last night, and she lay there with it going at full head all night." Clerk " Great heavens, man ! But why should you want to thank us?" Citizen : "You see, there was so little gas in the air which came from the pipe that it never hurt her a bit."

A MISrAKE.—The Sunday school teacher had reached a point in the lesson where she was dwelling upon the future reward of those who be- haved properly here, when the audacious small boy who frequents most Sunday schools spoke up and asked if all good people went to heaven. "Certainly," replied his teacher. " Well, has My grandmosher gone to heaven 1" persisted the youngster. "Surely she has, my boy, if she was a good woman." "No, she has'nt," declared the fun-loving youngster ; "there she is, over there !" The teacher turned to other phases of the lesson. "I wru, not deny, Mr. Ha rkalong," the young woman said, with downcast eyes, "that your attentions are agreeable to me. I—l am always glad to see you." Mr. Harkalong attempted to shorten the distance between them. "And yet," she went on, restraining him by a gesture, "I hardly know my own mind. I"-- "Miss Gillenwaters—Bertie !" interrupted the young man. "Never mind your mind. Listen to your heart. !" "That's what I am trying to do." she reph„J. "If I could only "-- "If you could only be sure I am worthy? Of course, I'm not, dear! No man a earth is good enough " "No, it isn't thil . 4g Your people object?" "Oh, no!" "Neither do mine!" he exclaimed, rapturously. Again he attempted to shorten the distance, and again she restrained him. " Bertie Gillenwaters," hoarsely he asked, "would you miss me if I never came here again?" "That's it, Mr. Harkalong," murmured the agitated maiden, looking at him with tears in her eyes. "I don't want you to stop coming. Indeed, I don't. I should miss you. Indeed, I should! Mr. Harka- long "—and a tear rolled down her chlek—" you bring me the best chocolate creams I ever get 1"

div.head: LADIES' LETTER:
div.p: LADIES' LETTER:

MY DEAR NELLIE, I think that both hats and toques are exoeesi- ingly attractive this season. The former are large and picturesque, chiefly of drap de feutre in some light colouring, such as strawberry-pink, heliotrope, sky- blue, or cream. The crown and brim form a plateau, fantastically crumpled of soft birciss plumage. The modified three-cornered shape is well worn, the point coming low down in the centre of the forehead, and the sides keep close to the head. It is not becoming to every face, but very stylish on those whom it really does suit. To be well worn, the hair must be well puffed out at the Bides. For an everyday hat, to be worn in all weathers, the straw toque triffmed with loops and rosettes in black or coloured straw cannot be too highly praised. This trimming is lighter than any other, and cannot be injured by rain or wind. Many hat-pins cannot hurt it, and its lightness saves its wearer from the ignominy of a crooked headgear, the depth of which only a woman can fully realise. There is, I may remark, a great feeling for beige and castor tones, both for hats and gowns. Some of the prettiest hats are made in two shades of castor only, and, of course, birds' plumage is a complimentary colour, and therefore is a good deal employed. Castor-brown also goes well with gold, which figures in moderation on many of the newest models.

Revivals are constantly brought to our notice and among the latest for this season is that of woollen lace. It is chiefly seen in tones of beige and tan-colour, and is excellent for yokes and sleeves of woollen blouses, otherwise rather likely to be dowdy of aspect. A warm woollen blouse for morning wear is an excellent thing, and a little smartness imported into it helps to cheer the thoughts of the wearer with the winter before her. A vizella blouse in tones of cornflower blue or wistaria mauve can very suitably be trimmed with woollen lace laid over silk or satin. It is a mistake to make the.sleeves too tight. The fashion ordains that they shall be close-fitting from the shoulder to the elbow, but there is an art in cutting this part of a gown which makes it look tight without actually being so. This implies skill, and skill means an expensive dressmaker. The cheap little worker cannot be expected to achieve this consummate union of apparently opposite qualities.

Tmid see shrill winds of October, furs are now not only talked about; they are a necessity. The bolero is so übiquitous that of course it has already appeared in mink and broadtail, with a lovely Tam O'Shanter to match, stuck through with a couple of new painted velvet quills starting from a rosette of the same. The sleeves of such a bolero and of the many coatees and longer wraps seen, are wide, opening above the wrists to show do.inty sleevelets beneath. Of lace or panne now, *esti must soon be of fur, and very snug and handsome they will be as the accompaniments of fur-trimmed velvet or cloth jackets.

If only skirts for walking dresses were a little shorter, the present fashion would be a very fairly sensible one. The skirt hangs in uninterrupted folds from the waist, with no superfluity of orna- ment. The very most that is ever applied is a deep flounce, sometimes shorter in front than at the back, but quite as often of an equal depth all round. Nor is there much exaggeration about the revers, so far as the shape is concerned. Three are a rather superfluous allowance, it is true, but the triple revers is usually so cleverly cut that it appears to be in perfect taste. The tendency of the hour is to give undue prominence to the front of the bodice. This is the chief fault of the fashion at present, with the overlong skirt. Of thick cheviots and tweeds there are plenty of dresses being made, with big storm coats to match and toques that recall to niemory the " darkie " handkerchief caps popular years ago. Such gowns are cut of a practical length, and there is a very sensible diminution in the inches given to all out- of-door frocks. Moreover, it is not correct to let them trail. _ _

Instead of buttons, silk tassels are I,eirr, used to make a diversion. These, it is almost certain, will give place to the pretty drop buttons that have been from time to time so charming an accompani- ment of a well-thought-out toilette. The drops are translucent crystals imitating emeralds, amethysts, and pink and yellow topazes. Pearls, too, may be employed with considerable charm. Jewelled buttonholes go with them, rimmed round with gems like the drops that fall from the centre. Of course, the whole thing is merely an imitation of buttons and buttonholes, but for all that, it is strikingly decorative and altogether delightful. Your loving JENNIE.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

In the fashionable world, that terror among women— the word dowager—has almost reached vanishing point. The Empress Frederick, our own Princess Royal—whose serious illness is causing her family so much anxiety— doomed the term, when she insisted upon taking the name of her dead husband as the definition to distinguish her from the wife of her son, and among those royal ladies, quick to follow her lead may be mentioned the widowed Czarina, invariably styled "Empress Maria Feodorowna," and the ex-Regent of the Netherlands, who is officially known as "Queen Emma"—Less distin- guished women have long availed themselvas of the chance to avoid so disagreeable a designation, and the word dowager is rarely whispered nowadays, and never by any chance does it appear on visiting cards. The Grand Duchess Serge of Russia—second daughter of the late Princess Alice—revels in the unostentatious life she leads when in Paris, and this country, and already appears stronger and less wan, than when she arrived. Stately in demeanour, and invariably dressed in perfect style, Her Royal Highness looks every inch a Russian Grand Duchess, and despite her not altogether happy life, is still a supremely beautiful woman. The Grand Duke Serge, who possesses a very fine presence, but a not very prepossessing expression, is an uncle of the present Czar. The Grand Duchess Elizabeth is there fore by virtue of her marriage aunt to her own sister the Czarina.

"lam of opinion that learning is necessary to the happiness of women, and ignorance the common found- ation of their errors, both in morals and conduct." These words of his ancestress—Lady Mary Wortley Montagu—the late Marqcis of Bute applied vigorously to his only daughter, Lady Margaret Stuart, the sharer of all his hobbies, and a most brilliant scholar. The late Lord Bute was married in 1872, and the ceremony which was performed by Cardinal Manning and Mon- signor Capel, created a great sensation, in soma degree due undoubtedly to his association in the public mind with the hero of Disraeli's novel. The present Marquis who is but nineteen years of age, is particularly keen on all kinds of sport, and of much leas studious disposition than his younger brothers, Lord Ninian and Lord Colu m Stuart.

_ The" Hall of Fame." which Miss Helen Gould has presented to the New York University, is just new the subject of a lively controversy in America. It has places reserved for the names of 150 of the most dis- tinguished Americans of whom fifty are to be selected at once, and five more every year until the year 2000. The decision rests with one hundred judees, and fifty- one votes are necessary for enrolment. None but Ameri- cans, and who have not been dead ten years or more are eligible for selection, and no business man or missionary, or explorer, can be nominated. As yet the judges are so little of one mind, that er..,arcely any name has received the necessary 51 votes, nor is this want of unanimity surprising, when we consider our own squabbles as to whether or not there should be a statue ot Cromwell in the House of Commons.

That the currant crop in Greece. upon which we de- pend for fruit for oat Christmas puddings, has been almost entirely destroyed by blight, is bad news. Very few people have as yet made their puddings and mince- meat, and it is expected that, for ordinary purchasers at Christmas, currants will be fully is 3d or is 61 per pound, or even more It is always a mistake to put off buying Christmas fruit until the dearest season of the year, and housewives would do well to lay in their stock before it goes still higher in price. Properly stored in jars, currants will keep for months, and even years, as fresh as when they were bought. Fortunately raisins, and sultanas are as yet only slightly affected by the scarcity of currants, and though like everything else. the Christmas pudding will cost more this year, it is to be hoped that the difference will not be so great as to seriously diminish it in BIZ 3 and quality. We ought to have a more cheerful Christmas this year than on the last occasion when we were in the dark days of the war. The return of the troops and the ill-feeling towards us, on the Continent, which the coming of Mr Kruger will be sure to revive, will tend to keep people at home. The war,in fact, has done much to solve the vexel question "Where to winter," and, as was the case last year, may people who usually go to the South of Europe, intend to stay at home, or winter at the more genial of the health resorts of Deyonahire and Cornwall, such as Torquay, Falmouth. Newquay, and Penzance. These places afford the invalid all the benefits of a mild and equable climate, without the drawbacks of a long journey to the Mediterranean, and the excellent train service of the Great Western Railway brings them within easy reach of London and of visitors from the North and Midlands.

Shopping proceeds gaily, and a particularly interesting occupation it is, for autumn and winter clothe; are very fascinating. There are ale aye several sew colours each season, and one in great request at the moment is a rich soft brown. That the shade is becoming to the genera- lity of women, there can be no possible doubt. More- over it is very accommodating, according as it does so admirably with mandarine yellow, and contrasting so effectively with pale green ; while seal, sable, mink, and chinchilla, make the harmony of the contrast even more delightful. There is no fur which brightens and smarten; up a gown, slightly relieved with white so successfully as does chinchilla, and by those women who are lightening their mourning this autumn, and can afford it, this particular fur premises to be extensively patronised. Unfortunately, it is costly, and, unlike several other (xpensive furs, does not wear well. It so soon gets grimy when taken out of doors, and once its freshness is tinged its beauty has quite gone. Instead of looking smart, it looks dowdy and shabby. It is therefore for the wealthy only. Blouses and shirts to go with tailor-made coats and skirts are very bright and fascinating, the favourite material for the former being perhaps printed panne. This fabric can now be had in the most delightful eatterns at the very moderate figure of 2s 11d per yard. Panne ribbons are quite a novelty. These are being shown in the loveliest of pale tones, richly embroidered in gold thread. For waist belts, collar and cuff facings, trimming toques and muffs, and divers other purposes these ribbons are invaluable, and will doubtless enjoy consideratle popularity during the coming winter. Several ministers at the Baptist Assembly admitted a partiality for tohaoco, but all agreed, as everyone does, as to the evil effects of cigarette smoking among young people. It seems to have been thought that the resolu- tion, condemning this practice, was as necessary in applying to girls as to boy; and youths. This probably goes beyond the tracts, as, though boys will smoke, girls usually wait nntil they are women as hen the habit may be vulgar and objsctionable, bu*: scarcely physically harmful.

But as regards boys it is urged by many medical men that the evil has become so wideipread, as to cAll for immediate and stringent legislation. The difficulty however would be to make any legislation effective. The bettor plan wru'd be for parents and schlrlmaAters to appeal to the boy's own sense of tho injury Le is doing himself, both constitutionally and by stunting his growth. In these days when all the rage is to excl at football and ithie c,ntests it is only newssary to

show a bop that he is really doing something fatal to his Physical development, in order to make an effectual impression upon him. It is genet illy believed that it was only in these latter days that women began to smoke, but as a matter of fact the practice was a very general one in the 17th century. Prynne, the Puritan states that " ladies at the theatre were sometimes offered the tobacco pipe as a refreshment instead of apples" and a French traveller, writing in 167?, observes that in England smoking was a general custom among women as well as men,and that children were taught to smoke by their mothers. This however, was no doubt partly due to the belief in the medicinal virtue aof tobacco. At the time of the Great Plague it was commonly reported that no tobacconists cm members of their households were affected by the pestilence, and consequently everyone was advised to smoke.

Yes, indeed, I must have it trimmed." "There are people—" "And he is unwell so often. But the bird man told me that a genuine poodle is always likely to be so." THE HOUSE BY THE MEI
BY MRS. C. N. WILLIAMSON, Author of "The Secret of the Pearls," "The Honse by the Lock," "Queen Sweetheart," "The Barnstormers," "Tier Royal Highness," &C.

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS: Lancelot Wade, a well-connected ne'er-do-well, lives with his daughter Sybil in fourth-floor rooms in Blooms- bury. One day the fatie-Ir [rings Sybil the extra- ordinary news that she— she who never went anywhere or saw anybody in her life—is to go to a dinner-party at Lady Nortimoilr's house in Berkeley- square, where she meets a c,.?rt.i4in Jack Churchill, who is expected by Lady Carstairs, another guest, to marry her daughter Gladys. The dinner, like the house, is very graod, Sybil is supremely uncomfortable. Next morning Lancelot Wade does not appear at brelklioit: Sybil finds that his bed has not been slept in. Alarmed, she is about to go to the police-station, when a messenger-boy appears with a letter from 4er father. The envelope is blood-smeared, and the aiessenger hesitatingly admits that he thinks there has been an accident. Sybil is conducted by tht messenger-boy, by means of trains and trains, quit Dut of the city to a lonely house on the river bank. She is told to enter a certain room, and, expecting to see her father, she unhesitatingly enters. The room is empty! And Sybil, when she tries to get out, finds herself a prisnrwr.

div.head: CHAPTER VI.
div.p: CHAPTER VI.
WHAT JA C= CHURCHILL READ IN TIIE NEWSPAPERS.

"Speshull extry speshul ! Hall abaht the rilewye accident and the suicide in the Thames!" Jack Churchill was walking down Northumber- land-avenue. He had bachelor chambers in White- hall-gardens, and he was going home to dress for a dinner he was giving at the Savoy Hotel in honour of Gladys Wade's ,birthday. He heard the news- boy's shrill shouting, without being conscious that he heard, until a grimy youth suddenly waved a print-sheet temptingly under his eyes. " Evenin' Yews! Extry speshul I Do 'aye one, sir!"

Jack had no particular desire to read the details of a railway accident and a river suicide; but the newsboy had tired, hungry eyes, and, flinging him a shilling, the young man found a paper thrust into his hand. He was passing under the bright glare of an electric light, and a name in the midst of a headline paragraph seemed to start up in his eyes. By Jove!" he exclaimed, and stopped under the lamp. "Supposed suicide in the Thames," he react "Pathetic letter.—While patrolling the Pool thi_ afternoon, between the hours of five and six, the vigilance of a police-boat was rewarded by a startling discovery. The body of a tall, strikingly, handsome man, approaching middle age, fashion- ably dressed in evening clothes, was found floating in the water. The coathad the name of an Austrian tailor inside the collar, and the pockets were empty, with the exception of a letter, probably identifying the corpse, as well as pointing to death by suicide, and supplying a motive. The body had evidently been in the water for at least twenty- four hours; but the letter, in a thick, linen-lined envelope, is still legible. The contents are as follows :

"Life has become too difficult. I find myself penniless and deeply in debt. Were I out of the way, the only person who depends upon me Would be cared for by relatives, as she never could be during my worthless life. It was with the idea of leaving her among those who would give shelter and kindness that I came to England; for the first time in many years I have been a failure, and dis- graced those who would otherwise have been my friends. The best thing I can do is to leave a world where I have done nothing but mistakes. That by this last step I retrieve some of them is the hope of Lancelot Wade."

It was the name which had caught and riveted Jack Churchill's attention, and he had gone back to the beginning of the paragraph to read down to the signature of the dead man's letter again, with a grave face. _ .

IlLancelot Wade ? " he repeated to himself. "Dead—killed himself? I should have thought he was one of the last men to do that! Ile seemed to be full of the joy of life—careless of everyone's welfare except his own. And yet he seems to have died with some idea that it is for his daughter's sake." Jack read on to the end of the paragraph which finished with a few words about the Hon. Lancelot Wade, his past, and his distinguished relatives; then, crushing the paper into a coat-pocket, walked slowly on towards the Embankment. He was thinking of Sybil Wade, the girl he had met at Lady Northmuir's three nights ago. He had thought of her often since then; but now a great pity filled his heart, and he felt oddly excited as well. He wanted to see her again; he wanted to be able to do something for her. This dinner which he was to give for Gladys had been arranged a week ago—one evening when she happened to mention, with apparent carelessness, that her twentieth birthday was due in a few days; and since seeing the little, poor relation, with sweet, pale face and wistful eyes, he had suggested that she, too, should have an invitation. But Lady Carstairs had said that Lancelot Wade had not chosen to give his aadress—probably he had his own reasons. Besides, she understood tho Lancelot and his daughter were leaving town almc,.. at once—perhaps had already gone. Therefore, it was hardly worth while to trouble. Jack Churchill's heart ached now as he thought of the young girl—so utterly alone. What must she not have suffered during the past few days, while he had been fancying, from Lady Carstairs's words, that she and her father were probably travelling away from London? Perhaps all this time she had been wild with doubts and fears for her father, while she was left alone in some gloomy lodging-house, believing herself deserted. Of course, now that this shocking affair had happened, the Carstairses would find her out at once, and do everything for her that could be done; but he wished desperately that he might have some part in the work. How awful it would be for the poor, desolate child if she had to find out the sorrow that had come upon her through some such paragraph as he had just read in the newspaper! Her image bloomed like a lily in his thoughts, and he could hardly bear lo know that so white, so delicate a flower of girlhood was beaten down by stress of storm. Jack's impulse always was to shield and protect those who were weak or forlorn; but never had he felt so strong a personal desire to help. He was glad now that Lady Carstairs had asked him to invite no one but themselves to this birthday-dinner, though, at the time, he would have preferred having one or two outsiders. Nov, it might be that, without seeming to drag a skeleL. to the feast, he might mention the sad fats of the- poor black sheep of the family, and hear what plans were being made for the girl. He did not expect much feeling from Lady Carstairs or Gladys for the unfortunate man who was dead, as there had never been affection, and very little acquaint- ance, between them; but he assured himself that, being women, their hearts would yearn over Sybil in her grief. "Carstairs will have heard of what has happened, of course," he reflected, when he had reached home, and was hurriedly getting into the things laid out by his man, to make up for lost time. "For the credit of the family, whatever his private sentiments may have been, Carstairs will claim the body, no doubt, and do everything decently and in order. After all, the poor fellow was his uncle; and, if he had not been disinherited, Carstairs would have had next to nothing, according to the stories one hcars. Perhaps Lady Carstairs may feel that it won't be good form to turn up at the Savoy with Miss Wade to-night, now one thinks of it, considering what a lot of people will have seen the evening paper. I may get word from her yet— that I'm not to expect them." - - -

The eagerness died out of his face at the thought —not in fear of losing a few hours of the beautiful Gladys's society, but lest he 4hould fail to hear news of the insignificant little ousin. • _ . . .

The dreaded intimation did not come, however, and Jack set out for the , Savoy, where La Carstairs and Gladys had appointed to meet hiti? at half-past eight. Eis chambers were on tho second-floor of the big, handsome building in Whitehall-gardens, overlooking the Embankment, and directly below was a flat occupied by two men, whom Jack knew slightly, partners in a rich and well-known firm of solicitors. For the younger of these, Beauchamp Drake, Churchill had a some- what inexplicable dislike, and, seeing the doer of the flat standing half-open, as if someone were about to come out, or had just gone in, he hurried past, lest he should be overtaken. Outside he went more slowly, for he had started rather too early, and allowed himself too much time (if he did not care to have his waiting at the hotel prolonged unduly) for the short walk from Whitehall-gardens to the Savoy. '

His thoughts had gone back to Sybil Wade again, as he strolled along the Embankment, when a voice that he recognised broke into their midst. It was that of Beauchamp Drake, who had an affected drawl, which Jack hated; and the solicitor was evidently behind him, in earnest conversation with a friend.

"Thank goodness the fellow won't want to join me, if he happens to see wilt) is walking ahead of him," thought Jack; for Drake, who was known as a toady to those richer or higher in position than he, was in the habit of seeking the young millionaire's society when he could. Jack moved on a little faster; but the wind came from behind, and blew the voices of the two men audibly to.his ears, though they spoke in low tones. "The little traitor ! " Drake exclaimed. "But then, you were a fool to trust her! You should never trust anybody, my dear fellow!" "What? Not even you ? " answered another voice, with a cynical laugh. It seemed to Jack that these tones were more or less familiar also; but he could not fit them with a personality .in his mind. And, besides, the matter possessed not the slightest interest for him. He did not voluntarily listen, and did not care in the remotest degree what the two men might have to say to each other. He had no reason to suppose that they were discussing secrets, or affairs which they would not wish the ordinary passer-by to hear, though it was possible that, if they had remembered the carrying power of the wind, they would have subdued their tones, even by night, on the Embankment, where pedestrians were few. Jack had increased his pane; but the other two appeared to be inspired with a desire for haste as well, for they also were walking faster, and their words continued to reach him as distinctly as before. "Not even me ! " Drake answered his companion' 6 question. "I'm like every other man I ever knew. I have my price; but, for the present, I'm satisfied with yours. We're in the same boat now, sink or swim, my dear chap" (how often he had silkily called Jack his "dear chap," in just such accents, and how Jack had disliked it !), which gives you a certain pull over me. But, really, I did think that my advice would have made more impression upon you!" "One can't provide for every emergency," said the other, gruffly. "If only Anson could be squared, it would be all right, even now." (Anson was the senibr partner in the firm of solicitors of which Drake was junior.) "Unfortunately, that's one of the few things I can't manage for you," drawled Beauchamp Drake. "We must do the best we can without; and that best would have been excellent if it hadn't been that you—trusted a woman ! "

- "I thought you said every man had his price? Why not Anson ? " "Ah !no doubt he has. But I haven't, been able to find out the figure yet—that's the trouble. And what I can't do with him, my dear fellow, it's no use even your trying." "By Jove! This sounds rather steep!" Jack said to himself. "I wish they'd stop, or let me get ahead. I don't want to know anything about that bounder Drake's dirty work, though I always suspected he was capable of it. However, there's one comfort. In all probability appearances are deceptive, and if I knew the real subject of their talk, it would turn out to be the most ordinary commonplace thing in the world, quite different from the mysterious sort of plot one would fancy, to hear them without understanding what it's all about. I'm afraid I'm too quick with my dislikes; and, just because that sleek, smooth-voiced beggar has the faculty of rubbing me up the wrong way, I needn't spring to the conclusion that he's a scheming villain. Probably those two are chaffing each other about some deal on the Stock Exchange." He began whistling, to drown the words that would come knocking a his ears, since the couple seemed determined not to be outdistanced. But afterwards—long afterwards—when it was too late, he remembered this night,, with sharpest regrets fox his own punctiliousness.

A few moments more, and it was time to turn ofl the. Emb9.nkment. He passed up the side-street which wpuld lead him to the Savoy Hotel, and then, with, a sudden impulse, of which he was ashamed after he had yielded to it, he threw a quick glance over his shoulder. Already the pair, who had gone straight on, were nearly out of sight; but Drake's companion was on the right, nearest Jack, and, as the light of a street-lamp illumined the figure for a fleeting instant, Jaci Churchill opened his eyes in sudden astonishment. "I wonder if it really was he ? " was the slow question he asked himself. "It might easily have been a chance resemblance, at that distance. But, even if I-wasn't deceived, what does it signify I I've really heard nothing to prejudice me at all and, anyhow, it isn't my business." A day was to come when he would, perhaps, change his mind; but that time was not yet.
CHAPTER VII. THE MYSTERIOUS BUNCH OF ORCHIDS.

Jack Churchill reached the Savoy Hotel fifteeL minutes before the appointed time, as was only proper and right, according to his chivalrous ideas of the consideration to be accorded women; but he had waited nearly half-an-hour before Lady Carstairs and Gladys finally appeared. Gladys Wade was always exceedingly handsome, in a dark, statuesque way (almost too sumptuom and self-assured for a girl, if to find flaws in suet beauty as hers were not too fastidious) ; bui to-night she was more animated, therefore more charming. than usual. She usually had the air ol being indifferent as to whether others were pleased with her or not, as if she.took for granted the fact that the least look or smile from so gorgeous s young personage as she ought to be thankfully received. With Jack Churchill she deigned to be more human and girlish, however, and on this hes birthday night she shone in sunny radiance. Apparently she would shed no tears over the tragic fate of her uncle, Lancelot Wade; and Jack wondered, as he took the gloved hand that she held out, whether Gladys and her mother could have failed, as yet, to hear the news. But Lady Carstairs at once put an end to his doubts.

"So sorry to have kept you waiting," she said. "But you are such a good-natured young man with your friends, that you have spoilt us. I daresay you can fancy what caused our delay. We have had such a disagreeable afternoon, poor Gladys's birthday would have been quite spoilt if she had not had this evening to look forward to. That shocking affair of Lancelot Wade, you know. A miserable ending to a miserable life ! I have been upset, of course; but I implored Gladys not to distress herself, as, really, the man was a stranger to us. There is only the publicity, and a little unpleasant gossip which will doubtless play round our name in connection with his, for us to mind." "Horrid having a policeman coming to Lady Northmuir's," said Gladys, "even if he was in plain clothes ! I felt quite as if mamma and I were criminals, going to be taken away." Jack was evidently supposed to laugh at this idea, and he did contrive a somewhat pre-occupied smile, accompanied by an inarticulate murmur. The ladies did not care to leave their cloaks in the dressing-room. Possibly this was due to the pleasing knowledge that not one among all the beautifully-dressed women dining at the Savoy Restaurant that night was likely to have anything so absolutely perfect as their evening wraps, lately arrived from Paris. Lady Carstairs and Gladys always laughingly acknowledged that they were dreadfully extravagant; and it was fortunate that Carstairs gave them a generous allowance beyond their own means out of his abundance.

They were conducted to the table, which had been specially decorated with a thought for their pleasurel and sat down, throwing their cloaks over the chairs, for the sake of the beaming backgroundo made by the rich, deeply-tinted satin linings. "What lovely flowers !" said Gladys. "My favourite colours. I wonder if. you remembered that ? "

It would have been surprising if Jack had not remembered, considering that the girl had been at some pains to impress her tastes unon his recollec- tion on many recent occasions. Now she held up a bouquet of pink-and-white orchids, which she had been carrying. "And this ! " she went on, with an effect of hesitation. "It was sweet of you to send it for my birthday, and with such wonderful ribbons " _ _

71a-c—k- -flushed, and came very near staring. He had not sent Miss Wade flowers that day. He had meant to do so, and then forgotten all about it, as he might not have forgotten last week. Circum- stances seemed almost to have forced him into seeing a great deal of Gladys during this visit of hers to London. Almost without intending it, and scarcely knowing how it happened (though, perhaps, Lady Carstairs, and even the girl herself, could have told), be had found himself paying the popular beauty rather marked attention. Though he was far from being conceited, he had plenty of common sense--too much (not being actually in love with Gladys) to send her orchids tied with diamond-monogrammed ribbon. The bouquet she held smilingly out for his in- spection looked like the eift of an accepted lover—.

or, at least, one wtro wished, and nad reason to believe, he would be accepted—to the one girl be was proud to honour beyond all others, in the eyes of the whole world. So that it was swag wonder Jack Churchill flushed, and began to feel as uncomfortable as he had ever been in his twentr eight years of life. The orchids were held tegether with gold-woven ribbons; and the glittering strePiners, edged with diamonds that scintillated like dewdrops under tha light of the softly-shaded candles, had, at regular intervals, all down their length, an elaborate alter" - nation of lovers'-knots and the monogram "G. W. in brilliants. It was a pretty, as well as costly, conceit; but Jack was not in precisely the mood to admire it. "This is far, far too handsome a present for you to have sent," said Gladys, "and mamma was going to be cross, 'and not let me accept it at first. 13(4 it was so pretty, and I wanted it so -much, and you are such an old friend of ours now, you know. Besides, it was clever of you, if you wanted me t 0 have anything so charming from, you, to apologise for it with flowers. There's no one else from who I could have taken such a thing Are you olesseu with that speech?" - Jack was very much embarrassed—more embar rassed, a great deal, than he had been in the Rockies a few months ago, when a grizzly bear had unexpectedly joined him in a stroll, finding hirn with no weapon save an American bowie-knife. It seemed horribly ungracious, when Gladys ha' just announced that nobody but Jack Churchia would have been permitted to send her such a gift" that he should coolly inform her it had, neverthe' less, come from someone else. Still, it was not fair to her, or to the giver, that he should accept a credit—a kind of responsibility—that did lot belong to him. "I—er—really, I'm afraid—" he stamn3erear as only a frank and honest-minded fellow, unspoilt by the world, ever does stammer. "I wanted awfully to send you some flowers to-day, you know, but somehow—"

• A spark lit up Gladys Wade's great dark eY,Leg' under the heavy white lids, that drooped at we outer corners. "What t" she exclaimed. *Did you send me th,.° orchids? Is that what you are trying so hard l° say, Mr. Churchill ? " "I can't, unfortunately, claim the credit such an original idea." And he glanced at the go,A streamers, with their conspicuously-arranged lovers • knots and monograms. • "Oh!" Gladys did not blush; but she droPPed her head, until the white parting that lay like e moonbeam along the dark chestnut hair was visible to Jack's eyes. "How ashamed I am! Somebodl has played me an unkind, hateful trick! Var, card was in tho box. Mamma, what shall I do? , "Nothing—nothing, of course, my dear child! soothed Lady Carstairs. "Don't be so distressed, or you will make Mr. Churchill, as well as rue, quite unhappy, I'm sure. This concerns him. 0° will find out who has taken his name in vain, lu such an inexcusable manner, and then we will send the ribbons and the horrid diamonds faded orchids and all !—back to the offender. But the curious thing about it is, now that I come to think of it, there was no florist's name on the box nothing by which to trace it. Don't you remember, Gladys, I spoke of that at the time it came? it has been a most expensive, as well as cruel, jest. for I don't see, after all, how we are ever to return the sender his property." "I will try—" Jack began, uncomfortably, when Lady Carstairs cut him short. "If you don't mind Mr. Churchill, I think W 0 won't speak of this any more at present. 13°1 little Gladys I'm afraid she's rather upset. An this is her night, you know. You and I will have a little talk about the myster—to-morrow, perhapsø if you have an hour disengaged in the morning, about twelve. That's right, Gladys, put the hateful bouquet out of sight! Its charm's gone And now we'll talk of something else--anything--- these delightful oysters, if you like.." Jack caught at the permission to change the subject, and, with more eagerness than tact, availed himself of this first opportunity to speak of whet was in his heart. "I wanted to ask you, if you don't mind," h,e said, "somethi„ng about your niece, Miss SYbu Wade." Lady Carstairs's thin eyebrows came togetho.e_r almost imperceptibly, though she gave a little lauoh as she answered: n aunt "Oh, pray don't give me the dignity (3- a d,s, where she is concerned. She was ray husban niece, unfortunately; but I didn't count her as mine!" Gladys was eating creme d'asperge, which just made its appearance, and did not speak. Dt;11 the tips of her pretty ears had suddenly torga pink, as they had a way of doing if she was elc':-ds or vexed. She had some thoughts about the orcin and their gorgeous accompaniments, which would have astonished Jack Churchill exceediugAY to hear. She had been much annoyed that he 110 talked to the little poor relation at Lady No muir's, when he might have talked to her. ; was still more incensed now that, after claw,' denying the gift of flowers, he should at once tura to a discussion of Sybil Wade's affairs. Altogether. the girl was in a very unbirthday-like humour. If. instead of spitefully breaking the crisp end of * sinner-roll with her strong, tapering fingers, she 3ould have nipped off the ell ofpoor Sybil's prettl Little straight nose, and so spoilt the child's beauty till the end of her days, she would at that moment aheerfully have done it. "No, of course, Lady Carstairs," Jack was quietly continuing, unconscious. of the storm in Gladys'S breast, "she is not related to you by ties of blood. But she seems to be left so completely alone in the world, judging from the few little confidences she Let slip the other night. Now that her father 110 30 suddenly been taken from her, I h tve beell wondering what would be her fate. No doubt. however, your kindness of heart will find adme waY put of her difficulties." Lady Carstairs looked up, straight into Jack's ayes. Her thoughts, if he could haveeread thenji would have surprised him even more than be laughter's. But he could not read them; he could mly see that something was mysteriously wrong.
(7o be continued.)

div.head: INTERESTING WEDDING AT GRAPPENHALL . CHURCH.
div.p: INTERESTING WEDDING AT GRAPPENHALL . CHURCH.

Th 3 quiet of peaceful Grappenhall was disturbed. lt.tst Thursday afternoon when considerable commo- ,tlol3 was occasioned by the marriage of Mr: Leonard Aiag Wilkinson, of Middleworth, solicitor at Black- burn and Clitheroe, to Miss Elizabeth Pigot, daugh- ter of the late Mr. James Cresswell Pigot of Liver- Pool and Southport: From the flagstaff on the tower of the ancient church, the flag of St George floated §ailY in the breeze. Thera were also displays of untiug in several places in the village whilst at the house of Mr. Arthur Pigot (the bride's hrother) at "Greenback," line 3 of flags stretched la various directions and presented a gay appearance. Villagers and people from the neighbourhood commenced to assemble at tho .Church long before the appointed time Or the ceremony, viz 2 o'clock. The guests Were accommodated with seats in the church and •"ir, W. Asquith Wood, the organist, played several voluntaries. On the arrival of the bride he played ,Lnliengrin's s Bridal March." The bride was charm- ingly attired in a dress of white satin, trimmed With duc'nes:43 lace and chiffon fichu. She wore a Wreath of orange blossoms and tulle veil. She carried °lovely bouquet of lilies of the valley, roses and carnations. There were six bridesmaids in attendance, viz, Miss May Pigot, Miss Marjorie Pigot. miss Eleanor Pigot, Miss Gertrude Pigot. misses Lilian and Fannie Ainsworth, alecee of the bride. They wore dresses Of white chine silk, trimmed with insertion, chiffon fichu and blue panne bows,and black picture hate. Their bouquets were composed of lilies of the Valley, and pink carnations tied with blue ribbons. The duties of best man were satisfactorily dis- charged by Mr W King-Wilkinson, jun, brother of the bridegroom. The service was fully choral and the surpliced choir led in the sing- ing of "The Voice that breathed o'er Eden and 0 Perfect Love." The ceremony was Performed by the Rev J C Pigot and the Rev H Pigot (brothers of the bride), assisted by the Rev Richard Greenall, rector of Grappenhall (cousin of the bride), and the Hey R D H Gray, vicar of Chat- burn, near Clitheroe. At the conclusion, Mendels- sohn's well-known" Wedding March "was played, and as the tnewly-married couple left the church the bells rang out a merry peal. A reception was afterwards held in the school- room which had been tastefully decorated for the occasion. A large number of guests were present and an opportunity was afforded of inspecting the choice presents which had been arranged on tables running down one side of the room. Mr aril Mrs King-Wilkinson shortly afterwards departed for London and Cornwall where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride's travelling dress was of blue cloth (tailor-made) trimmed with white crepe de thine lace and large black satin stitched collar with black hat to match,

div.head: J__.4p.__ WEDDING AT FRODSHAM.
div.p: J__.4p.__ WEDDING AT FRODSHAM.
Lomas—Linaker.

The wedding took place on Wednesday afternoon at Frodsham of Mr A D Lomas, F. 5.1., and Mies Jennie Linaker. Both the contracting parties are exceedirealy well known in the district, and it is not, therefore,'to be wondered as that the event was a papular one and created widespread interest. The bridegroom is the assistant land and rating agent of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Company, and is the second son of the late Rev P Lomas, 8.A., of Liverpool, while the bride is the eldest daughter of Mr Charles E Linaker, F. 5.1., Frodsham. Unfortunately the day was hardly in keeping with such an auspicious event. The weather was cold, and the flashes of sunshine weie followed by heavy showers of rain. Still the somewhat inclement weather did not prevent the townsfolk from journeying to the church to witness the ceremony. To while away the time as the wedding guests were taking their seats, the organist, Mr C H Hibbert, played choice selections of music, which included The Bridal Marc " Lohengrin " (Wagner), " Arm of the Lord" (Haydn), " Marche aux Flambeaux " (Clarke), and Meiadelssohn's " Wedding March." Promptly at two o'clock the bride, leaning on her father's area, arrived followed by her bridesmaids. She was joined at the altar by the bridegroom, who was accompaniel by Mr Thomas E Lomas, as best man. The bridesmaids, six in number, were Misses Alice Linaker (sister of the bride), Mary Lomas (sisterof the bridegroom), Frances Limiest*, Lora Linaker, Mary Allsupp, end Marian Gregson (cousins of the bride). They all locked exceedingly pretty, their dresses being composed of sehite China silk. trimmed with Valenciennes lace and insertion. They wore large white silk hats, which carried velvet trimmings, and they bore large yet neat bouquets composed of white flowers and autumn leaves. They also displayed handsome pearl and turquoise horse- shoe brooches, tbe gift of the bridegroom. The bride looked charming in a gown of ivory brocade trimmed with white chiffon, orange blossom and white heather. She wore a tulle veil, which was crowned by a wreath ' of orange blossom, and carried a white bouquet, the gift of the bridegroom. The clergy and the surpliced choir led the way down the aisle, singing " The voice that breathed o'er Eden," The marriage service was then most impressively conducted by the Vicar of Frodsham, the Rev H B Bloieg, assisted by the Rev It Cuffs, vicar of St Stephen's, Edge Hill, Liverpool. After the parties had plighted their troth Ps4ll/1 xlviii was chanted, and, preparatereeto signing the register, the hymn commencing "How welcome was the call " was heartily sung by the congregation. As the newly- wejded pair left the church the organ poured forth music, the bells pealed and the sun which had hitherto been clouded over, beamed smilingly upon them. After the wedding breakfast had been partaken of at Mr C Linaker's houee,the happy couple left for London and the south coast. The briste's travelling costume was of dark grey with a black velvet picture hat. The cabs were supplied by Mr W Youd,Bear's Paw,and the hand- some weeding cake by Mrs Jane Bibby of Frodsham.

div.head: FOREIGN MISSIONS.
div.p: FOREIGN MISSIONS.
Enthusiastic Meeting in the Parr Hall.

To 'celebrate the bi-centenary of the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts, a public meeting was held in the Parr Han on Tues- day evening. The building was completely filled, and the meeting was a pronounced success. A choir drawn from the different churches in the town occupied seats on the platform and led the singing of the hymns. Mr W 9 Wools, late organist of the Parish Church, presided at the organ with his customary ability. The chair was occupied by the Lord Bishop of Liverpool (the Right Rev Dr (Jhavasse) and amongst those present were the Rev A G Lewis (late Arch- deacon of Bombay), the Rev J W Stenson (from Bloemfontein), the Rector of Warrington (Rev Canon Willis), and the Revs EC E Carleton, Morley Stevenson H A Lester, E R Tarbuck, F T. Powell, W J H G Rolling worth, II R Wild, J R Jones (Great Sankey) 17 R Matthews (Earles- town), A F White, G W Dickinson, W Bracecamn, A S Cameron, L W Thomas, Majlr J D Buckton, Mr H J Westbrook, and others. The p&-oceedines Com- menced with the singing of the hymn "Thou whose Almighty word "after which the Rector engaged in prayer. Tee CHAIRMAN in the course of his remarks said he thought nothing was more remarkable then the change that had taken place in the atticu ie of Eaelishmen to- wards foreign missions. He could remember the day when the" Times "newspaper was scathingly sarcastic abut missionaries and missions. He had lived to see the day (last year) when the" Times " published a long and appreciative article on the work of the C.M.S.; and this year an equally appreciative article upon the work of the S.P.G.—(applause)—while only that day in the "Times," one who was not usually regarded as a great friend of missions in China, spice with the utmost plainness upon the Russel:ire of missionaries, and demanded England as a nation to take note of the matter. And he noticed the same great change in their statesmen. A hundred years age the Govern- ment of India refused to allow a missionary to land upon its shores, and the first E welsh missienary had to settle in Dinish India ; and Henry Martin, when he devoted his life to great missions, could not go out as a missionary, but as a chaplain of the East India Company. They had lived to see great statemen like Lord Lawrence and Lord Northbrook stand up in the midst of their metropolis and speak in no measured language upon the importance and success of missions in India; and when they turned to the church they found the same remarkable change. When first of all the Church of England awoke to its position in regard to Christian missions not a single Englishman could be found who was ready to go out, and he helieved he was right in saying that the first missionaries troth of the S.P.G. and C.M.S. were not Englishmen but Germans— not English clergymen but Lutherans. To-day the greatest advocate of Christian missions in the Church of England was their Primate—(applause)—who never spared himself when he thought be could promote the cause of the English mission to the heathers. When they asked what was the cause of that remarkable change he thought they might say it was due firstly to the logic of facts, and secondly to the enlightenment of the public conscience. It was due first of all to the logic of facts, and impar- tial observers had not been able to deny the remarkable success of Christian missions. Charles Darwin, to whom they owed the theory of evolution, might not be regar- ded as a great advocate of missions, but se struck was he by the marvellous results of the South American mis- sionary societies' work in Patagonia that throughout the rest of his life he became a regular subscriber to its funds. Stanley, in his book " Darkest Africa," spoke of the marvellous success of the mission in Uganda. On Monday evening it was the privilege of some of those on that platform to listen to a remarkable speech of Sir Charles Turner, late Chief Justice of Madras. He told him (the Lord Bishop) before the meeting began, that it was his delight to go about wherever he could and tell the English public what the missions were doing in India. To-day they looked upon the Fiji Islands, once cannibal islands, as Christian upon vast tracts in Southern India, where the natives had been gathered in bythousands and tens of thousands, and it was once his lot to hear that remarkable u.an Sir Bartle Frere liken Christianity in India to a ship which for years had been locked in by the ice, but just as when the first breath of spring passed over the Arctic waters, the ice broke up and began to move, and the ship moved with it. So to-day in India the old faiths were gradually breaking up, and the ship Christianity was making slow but certain way in that great and glorious land. (Applause.) The second cause he thought was the enlightenment of the Christian conscience. They were coming more and more to realiz that there was such a thing as spiritual selfishness in keeping the good things of God to themselves. To-day the Church was repeating the words of et. Peter of old, "What I have I give." To-lay England was beginning to realize that God had made her what she was, not that she might wax fat and kick and find berths for her younger sons or amass mighty wealth, but that she might be God's great instrument for spreading abroad His Gospel to the great missionary church of the West. (Applause.) And lastly what were they to do ? There were three things he thought. First he would say "Read missionary periodicals." The k3owledge of facts was the great strength of missionary influence. Then they must give their men, women and money. Why, here in Lancashire there were thousands and tens of thousands who were living practically heathen lives. The question was asked "Are we to send our men and money abroad when to-day the number of candidates for holy orders is beginning to decrease and our clergy find it hard to obtain efficient workers for spiritual work ?" Yes, he said, for two reasons ; first because history told them this great fact—that no country was ever evangel- ised from a country that was completely evangelised it- self. When the church at Antioch sent out St. Paul and Sc. Barnabas the vast mast of the people were heathens still, but the little community, movea by God's Holy Spirit, gave its very best men to preach the gobpel to the heathen. When St. Patrick went out from Golloway and carried the gospel to the Irish the west coast of Scotland was still shrouded in darkness, but the Church gave him freely to evangelise a land that knew not God. When their own St. Aidan, a great and memorable figure in the history of their church, left lona there were islands and countries far nearer which as yet had not heard the name of Cnrist, but the little community of lona gladly gave its noblest members to bring the gospel to their own Northumbria. And the Church of England must not wait until she had made the Church of England the Church of the Eaglish, but in sending out her best men she would find that Gad would bless her at home. (Applause.) And "there is that scattereth and yet increaseth." A second ream was this—that when missions were not thought of a church was dead, and, in proportion as a church thought of missions that church lived. The church that received the blessing of God and kept it to itself would die. The church that received and gave out would live, grow and multiply; And, last of all, they must pray. Their blessed Lord taught them to pray for missions when He ' bade them say "Thy Kingdom come." As true children of the English Church, let their prayers seek to be as wide as the heart of God, and pray not only for their own family and neighbourhood, but gather in the whole world ; then by praying and learning, each one of Ahem would help to hasten the coming of that day "when the knowledge of the Lord should cover the earth as the waters cover the sea." (Applause.) The Yen. Archdeacon Lewis then delivered an eloquent address. He remarked that he had been wondering why there was little interest shown in missionary work. The Bishop had said that the interest was growing. He agreed. Nevertheless the problem still remained, why did "the man in the Street" take so little interest in missionary enterprise? That was more remarkable when one noted that the "men in the street" were so deeply interested in almost every other subject under Heaven. Why should people take so much interest in one thing and so little interest in another thing, when one was quite as important as the other? He had been told that it was strange that the laity took very little in- terest in missionary work. He was not quite sure that that was a fair way of stating the plaint, for he bad yet to learn that his reverend brethren and he himself were consumed with the flames of their enthusiasm in the cause of missions. How was it, therefore, that the people generally, both the clergy and laity, took so little interest in missionary work? They did not belong to a nation that was nig- gardly or unsympathetic to those who were in trouble,.

The characteristics of Eaglish men and women were pity and generosity. They tis.d to acknowledge that in view of the facts which came before them during the last few years. They rememberei that a few years ago when the cry came from India of a famine—stricken people thousands and hundreds of thousands sof pounds were poured into thelcoffers ef the Mansion House in London. He saw in his " Daily Telegraph" that millions of shill- ings had been subscribed for the refugees and for the wounded in that mournful war in South Africa, and he remembered the patience with which the country en- dured the increase of taxation in order that her Majesty's Miaisters might have thz wh rewithal to carry out the campaign to a successful iss se in order that the prestige and safety of the country might be assurred. (Ap- plause.) They knew that the heart of the nation was touched and the purse of the nation was opened. The heart of the nation was touched- Was not that the k le to the solution of the missienary problem It had not yet been touched on this question. When men and women of the country realizes that it was the duty of the whole nation to light for God as it was the duty of the whole nation to fight for Queen Victoria, then and then only might they look for great success in the campaign for God in toe mission field. (Applause.) The reason the heart of the nation had not been touched was because the brain of the nation had not yet assimilated those great principles which made rnission.aty work and interest not a matter of choice but a matter of duty. (Hear, hear.) fhe first of those pqaciples was that the Church of God was before all things a mission agency. Another was that ideally the Church was catholic, not in a narrow sense, but in a great and glorious meaning which belonged to it. It was cstholic because it was based upon the Incarna- tion. The Church was for all people for all time. A third principle was that missionary work was the work of everyone, not only of the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel, or the Church Missionary Society, or the work of the clergy : it was the work of the nation and the work of the whole church. (Applause). Ged had given Eneland its great position in the world, not that she should vaunt herself in the forefront of the nations of the world, not that she should have a name for great- ness and wealth, but so that she should bring souls to Him. That was the only way he read God's goodness to them as a nation. (Applause). This bi-centenary was a call to the nation to raise itself to its privileges, respon- sibilities and duties. (Applause.) The speaker re- ferred to the union between the Church and the State. There were some things which the Church could not do and the State Could do, and there were also things which the State could not do and the Church could do. What the thing was which they could not do in combination he had yet to learn. In conclusion he said that God was giving to us a large portion of South Africa and God had given to us that enormous continent of India. What had we done in the one, what were we going to do in the other. Were we going to be satisfidd with a civil Government with a secular education, or were we only going to be satisfied when they had woo these great nations into the service of Almighty God. (Applause.) In addressing them that night he appealed uot only to the religious element that was in them, but also to their patriotism. He loved God and he loved his country also. (Applause.) _

Another hymn was sung and a collection made for the bi-centenary fund, which amounted to £2l 43 101. The Rev J W STENSON in the course of a highly inter- esting address, said the S.P.G. was called into existence because of the religious needs and necessities of their own people when they left the shores of England and went into a foreign country. In England, where they had their daily services, and their weekly communions, they could not understand what it was to be suddenly put down in a place where there were no services, no sacraments, no clergy to be seen for many years. Inter- esting anecdotes were given by the speaker to show how interested the people of South Africa were in the work of the missionary societies. While they kept their church organization they did not allow their churchman- ship to interfere with their several qualities. It might be asked" Do you work together ?" In one way they did, but to ask a Churchman and those who were not Churchmen to work side by side was like asking Tories and Liberals in England to work side by side for political services. Ira Africa they did so, but the Liberals became Tories after they had been out there a short time. (Laughter.) He wished the clergy and parents here would take a lesson from their book in South Africa. The great fault was that they sent out their young men with a letter of introduction to Mr. Rhodes or some other influential man in Kimberley, or some banker, but there was never a letter of introduction to the clergy. In Basutoland, where he first began the work, there was not a single church, but now there were six churches and between 2,000 and 3,000 native communicants. In Kimberley they had three or four churches, a native church, and service was conducted in four languages. The great English nation had been called upon by Almighty God to exercise its right and responsibility in South Africa by placing those who were to rule over it in their proper position. A tremendous responsibility rested upon the English nation when they considered the .anative races in Cape Colony. The black man in the Transvaal would under- stand now that there was not only law, but such a thing as justice. (Applause.) In answer to Mr Stead's allusion to his "brother Boer" he had only to ray that when the Boer proved himself, unworthy to rule those who were weaker than himself that power must be taken from him and given to a nation who knew the meaning of justice and equality between man and man. (Applause.) The Bishop having to leave while the Rev gentleman was speaking, the chair was taken by the Rector. Major PgICKTON proposed a vote of thanks to the Bis- hop of Liverpool,lArchdeacon Lewis, and the Rev J W Stenson for their presence and speeches. Mr Wzmaroos seconded, and the motion was heartily carried. _ _ _ _ _ - _
The meeting concluded with the ainging of the National Anthem. _
171-a-e thanks of all interested in this gathering are due to the Rev H A Lester, lecturer at the Training College, who has acted as secretary to the committee.

div.head: BY-ELECTION IN BEWSEY WARD.
div.p: THE BY-ELECTION IN BEWSEY WARD.

As announced in our last issue, Mr T B Malkin will be the Liberal candidate in Bewsey Ward to fill the vacancy occasioned by the elevation of Councillor Shaw Green to the position of aldermen of the borough. Monday last was the last day for the receipt of nominations and it was found that Mr. Gough had once again entered the field for municipal honours as an in- dependent candidate. The Liberal candidate, Mr Thomas Broomhall Malkin, iron-worker, Liltord- street, who is proposed by Mr. Thomas Pemberton, seconded by Mr. William Ford, and assented to by Messrs. John Rudge, Edward Hardman, Thomas Atkinson, John Bennett, Fred Worsley Beech, Francis Worrall, James Harris and John Jones. In a second paper the candidate is proposed by Alr. John Waring and seconded by Mr. Joseph Parkes whilst in a third paper be is nominated by Mr, Samuel Archer and seconded by .Mr. Fred Highley. Mr. Samuel Gough, of 106, Winwick-street, abuse furnisher, has been nominated by Mr. Peter White, seconded by Mr James Ashton and supported by Messrs John Riley,John Lee,Robert Collart,William Riley, Henry Weaver Beddard, William Blease, William Taylor, and John Ashton. The election has been fixed for Monday next, the 22nd inst.
The Late Mr. Claude J. Morris.

Prior to the business of the Warrington County Petty Sessions being proceeded with on Wednesday morning, the Chairman (Mr. G. Comber) alluded to the loss the Bench had recently sustained by the death of Mr. Claude J Morris. Mr Comber observed that the death of their former colfcgue was a very sudden one, and he was sure all attending the Court, as well as the Bench, would regret it. All present stood while the above observations were made.
FURS. W. T. Williams has just received a choke stock of Furs, New Autumn Millinery, Gloves, Skirts ac, 74, SANKEY-STREET. Warrington.—Advt.
Ohmy's Circus.

This week Mr Ohmy, the popular circus proprie- tor, winds up his successful visit to Warrington, and Monday evening was tet apart as his" benefit night." The programme included several contests which were participated in by youths selected from the audience, and their crude attempts to perform on the low trapeze and the tight wire were the source of much merriment. A strong company of capable artistes appeared in new acts and their efforts were fully appreciated by the large audi- ence which assembled. Mons. Alvar went through a number of risky felts on the high wire fifty feet in length, concluding by carrying a youth across on his back. His performance is certainly well worth witnessing. The Padley Brothers were very successful in their difficult act on the staircase, and later in the evening the same artistes appeared as clowns. The ZJla troupe of acrobats displayed great skill, and the perch performance hy the Bros. liolliway was another capital "turn." Miss F Transfield earned hearty plaudits by her graceful bareback riding and young Itoberts rode splendidly in his jockey, act. A novel item was contributed by T B Gilbey, who gave a clever exhibition on an unsupported ladder. Mr Harry Dale maintained his popularity as a jester, and several other items constituted a first rate programme.

INFLUENZA AND INDIGESTION CURED AT
WARRINGTON.

There are plenty of engine drivers in Warrington, who have won their onerous positions by perseverance and hard work. It was with the driver of a yard shunting engine that a reporter of the " Warrington Examiner," recently had a conversation.

Mr. James Evans, 9, Wellfield-street, Warrington, is an engice-driver in the employ of Me.sssrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sans, Limited, one of the largest soap. making firms in the world. As he is 49 years of age be has had same caned- epee, and knows that the best of health is necessary for him to go through his day's work. Mr. Evans has not been favoured during the six or seven years he had been working at Warrington. He was troubled very much by indigestion, and pains in the side, for which he took much medical advice and a !large quantity of so-called curatives without deriving much benefit. Then, about tour months ago the influenza fiend claimed him 88 a victim and brought him down to such a low state that he was three weeks absent from work. In his own words, "I got terribly low, and always felt more tired when I had done nothing, than I should have done if I had done a laborious day's work. The pain in my side was there too. While I was in this state a pampelet entitled "The Way to Be We:l "was pushed under my door, and that gave me an idea. I !would try Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People. From the first I had faith in the pills, and by the time I had finished two or three boxes I felt much better and stronger. Before, I had not been able to keep warm, but now I got warmer and gained strength rapidly. The pain in my side went away altogether,eand I gained 61135. weight in six weeks. I have been better. in health since then than I have been all the six years I have lived in Warrington." Questioned more pirticularly about his indigestion trouble, Mr. Evans said he had not felt it since he took the pills, and "I can eat anything now. Thank G3d ! and sleep well too." He had, he said, recommended Dr. William' Pink Pills to several friends of his. His wife had been a great sugerer from sick headaches for many years and he had persuaded her to try the pills. Though she had only been taking them a short time she was already feeling considerable benefit.

The Warrington tam as a whole played a much better game than previously though whether tbis was due to the weakness of their opponents or not I cannot say. Future matches will show. 'Nero was more passing out and more combination of the sort that gets tries. Isherwood was in better form and this made consider- able difference, but he has a lot of ground to make up even yet. Fish was the bright partieu;ar " star,' and I cannot do better than quote what a Wigan writer says of him. "The Warrington wing three-quarter, how- ever, was a host in himself. He made one of the finest sprints witnessed on the Wigan ground, was at all times as nimble as a cricket, and the ‘l2 ay he danced round the Wiganers was a perfect treat for his admirers, but not for the home supporters."

The concluding remark is especially true. Both span- tators and players got exceedingly savage at Fish's elusiveness. Ho would not be tackled, and it was not. till about threr-quarter time that the Wiganers got a proper hold of him and grassed him prverly. Then such a cheer went up,as one might expect if Wigan had won. It was certainly Fish's day out, and if be is in similar fora% this Saturday, the Cumbrians will know about it.

The Warrington forwards also played splendidly, and were far the superior set in the open. Wigan had weight but lacked speed and skill. Bate and Burgess operated more effectually behind the pack, and are beginning to fit in better with each other. The right wing was safe, and the same may be said of Hallam who saved bis side more than once.

Eckersley, late of Tyldesley, was the only man on the Wigan side who showed conspicuous good f )rm. He is a very fair three-quarter. The others are decidedly amateurish, while at half, Owen and Middleton were below expectations. Nicolson has the ability to move his legs quickly and that is all.

The quarterly meeting of the Thelwall Parish Cbuncii was held on Monday evening in the Schools. Lu the absence of the Chairman (Mr Norman Taylor), wno is seriously ill, Mr Roebuck (vice- chairman) presided, and there were also present— Admiral Jones-Parry, Messts Astall, Tuck. Ford, Whitlow and Cook (clerk).—The Clerk reported that he had written to the Manchester Ship Canal Company with respect to the great inconvenience caused at Taelwall Ferry when school children especially bad to wait in the rain before Oey could go across the canal on the pontoon. He pointed out in a letter that a waiting-room on either bank was needed, and suggested a wooden structure. He had since received a reply to the letter stating that the matter would receive the attention of the com- pany. It appeared that the company bad sent hie letter to Captain Waring, who came to ask him what was wanted, and when he saw that the com- pany would not have to go to any great expense he said he would report favourably and added that no douot something would be done in the matter. Up to the present no eteps had been taken.—Mr. Tuck: It is a thing that is very much needed.— The Clerk read a letter from the Runcorn Rural District Council etating that the village footpath, would be repaired in due course.—Mr Astall moved that the attention of the Rural District Council be called to the unfinished state of the road leading to Massey Brook. de observed that rough stones had been thrown down on the road, but they had not been rolled to a smooth level. A great deal of in- convenierica bad been experienced by cyclists especially, for about four months, and it was time that a eteam roller was brought upen the scene.— Admiral Jones-Parry remarked that the Council had only just purchased a steam roller and he would see ii it could not be brought to Thelwall at once.— The Council had gone to great expense lately, and at such a time be did not think people should Cry oat too soon—Mr Astall: I have always thought that the CJuncil was in posses- sion of a steam roller, and under the circumstances I will withdraw my motion.— Admiral Jones-Parry made a few remarks with res- pect to the alleged nuisance at Grappenhall which, he said, had been mis-called the " Thelwall nuis- ance." The effluent from Messrs. Long's Tannery had been analyzed, and it was found to be very bad. That was in Grappenhall. The Sanitary In- spector had reported no nuisance from the property of Mr. Naylor. A cesspool had been found under the middle of the road, and that required prompt attention, but no one would own it, with the result that it had not been attended to. The newspapers had given the public a very erroneous idea of the matter.
