div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football. [By " Ovalist."]

The somewhat despondent admirers of the Warrington football team were inexpressibly cheered by the result of the match with Wigan on Saturday. They ieared that the said-to-be improved colliery brigade would just about rob Warrington of the two points gained tuere last season, but the locals rose to the occasion in a style which delighted their supporters. A victory of 16 points to 2 is at any time a rare accomplishment for Warring- ton, andisuch a triumph on Wigan soil was almost too good to be true—at least that was the opinion of those who stayed behind. The hundred or two who went away with the team saw ducks and drakes made of the Wigan defence, and the wonder was that the score did not top tne 6' twenty." But for a very troublesome cross-wind it probably would have reached this figure, for in open play the home lot were far behind their visi- tors.

A fatalist might see significance in the fact that Treasurer Pemberton accompanied the team, for on the rare occasions on which he has gone away with the players they have, so far as be can recollect, invariably won—barring cup-ties. I don't remember the last league match on foreign soil that had Mr. Pemberton as spectator, but if his presence is so good an omen as it beemed to be on Saturday he must go away oftener. We want somebody to "bring the luck," as it were

Warrington certainly had the luck on Saturday, for the home lull back played the wcrit game of his life, and Jact " Smith was in one ot his most favourable moods. The Warrington lads used to love other referees more than the Wicinesian whistle blower, but since his kindness at Broughton last year, when Burgess was allowed to score a startling off-side try,they have looked upon •' Jack" with more favourable eyes, I'm not sug- gesting that he inclines towards Warrington or any other club, in the least, but somehow he has uncon- sciously Gone the Warrington club more good turns in the, last two seasons than in the rest of his career. Ou Saturday J T Bate go.: one of the cheekiest tries be ever scored, and apparentiy Mr. Smith's blind eye was on that side for it was allowed.

You must not get the impression that the match was at all a run-away affilr, for the Wiganers bad as much of the play as their conquerors—in fact it is just a qUes- tion whether they did not spend a little more aim° in the Warrington half than in their own. Fr the whole of the first twenty minutes they were attacking more or less vigorously, and Wasrington could make no head- way. There was no serious danger, however, for the slowness of the home team in rLatters of combination made them easy to repel. During this period the übi- quitous Fish was starving on the touch line with no- Wing to do. The wind was blowing away from him and the Wigan men were very careful to keep the oval on the opposite side of the field. Consequently the " finny one " bad to change his tactic 3, arm by giving himself a sort of roving commission he found means to keep both himself and the Wiganers warm. He helped himself to the ball and soon had it nearer the home team's line. His example stirred Warrington up and before long they had the Wiganers cornered. Fish picked up smartly and finding Isherwood on the wing he gave the latter an easy try at the corner.

This score settled Wigan entirely. They seemed to fall to pieces, and before five minutes bad elapacd Mere- weather bad taken advantage of oue of And( rton's many mistakes and scored under the posts. Fish kicked a goal. Smart play on the Warrington side was now frequent, and before the interval Fish took a shlrp pass from Isherwood at half way and raced over, in a fashion which e:ectrifieci the crowd. To vary matters Isherwood took the kick and landed a second goal, making tha score 13-0.

The second half was inori! evenly contefeed and w•veral times Wigan came near scoring by E her forwarc, strength. Hallam was generally in the way, however, and all they got was a penalty goal. Warrington added another three points by the aid of Bite, who seem,d to put the ball in and take it out of the scrimmage all with

div.p: crisis passes away." All these circumstances will .tend to give vigour to the Opposition. The mo- ment any grave domestic change is proposed the 'Opposition can and will contend that the Govern- ment has exhausted its mandate, and was not em- Powered to deal with it at all. But it is said that there are discords in the Liberal party, and that its leader in the Commons is incapable of controll- ing it with strength and discipline. The basis for these assertions is the old Opposition. The new OPposition, however, has been strengthened by the addition of capable members, who have every in- -duceraent to engage in an active political war. As soon as the country sees that all imaginary dangers are over and that there will be no reversal of policy in South Africa, the Liberals will begin to win bye-elections bacause the country will have recovered from its fright and it will want substan- tial reforms. Sir H. CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN has behind him a compact body of adherents, and we shall look to him for a more resolute leadership and for more heroic opposition. In short, the -fears about a disorganised rabble on the Liberal .aide are groundless. There will be an early indica- tion as to the vigour and elasticity with which the OPposition will act.
THE order to Lord Roberts A Lagging War. to come home and take

over his new duties seems to have been withdrawn, and he is remaining in south Africa to bring matters to an end. It is now thought unlikely that he will be able to return for another three months. The argument that the Boers were watching our politics at horn e lind holding out in the hope of a change of Administration has now been replaced by a con- tention that they are waiting upon the success of Mr. BRYAN in the American Presidential contest, or the result of Mr. KRUGER'S mission to Europe. lie excuse of this kind will sufficiently explain the facts. The Boers are ignorant of what is going on outside South Africa. They are not influenced by anY of the considerations which seem to be so Plausible to other people. They are resisting because there is so little for them to gain by any Other course of action, and their plans have been laid for a guerilla warfare. The foreign con- tingents have been disbanded or destroyed. commandos now in the field are Boors) under their own leaders, and Boers who, having lost everything, are resolved to make our conquest as tedious and as expensive as possible. In many reePacts we have suffered from the want of a mili- tary uniform by the Boers, which renders it so 'easy to leave the fighting ranks and return to civil life, only to re-appear with rifles when a local danger has passed. Any other combatant would have compelled respect for the laws of war by deporting from a district any males who were sus- ected of having fought against us, and by order- fig that Boer combatants should wear some distinctive mark or costume. The Germans shot the francs-tireurs in France. We could not have ollowed the same policy in the Boer states, but We have probably been too lenient with many of them who made their submission and resumed their military activity the moment our backs were turned. The railways have, in most cases, been injured by local Boers, and the destruction of their houses has been a severity to which LORD ROBERTS has felt himself driven by facts. Rouses flying the white flag and yet used for firing upon our men have been fired. In this Way, we have probably increased the number of guerilla bands. The Boers themselves have hidden away in different centres supplies of arms and ammunition, and they are now falling back upon them. They have some bold leaders still at large, and they rally around them. Wher- ever they are marauding a state of terrorism exists, and peaceful burghers are compelled to assist. Until we can dispose of DE WET D , ELA.REY, and VILJOEN, we cannot hope to convince the guerillas that they had better resume civil life. The plan to be adopted is to divide the country infested by these bands into districts, each with a Mounted force and in communication with its neighbours. It is for this purpose that Lord ROBERTS has been consulting with his generals, and when the plan can be put into effective opera- tion the work of suppression and pacification will Make more satisfactory progress. When we can Protect the well-disposed as well as punish the guerilla bands, we shall be gradually reducing the country to order. It will be well for us not to be aanguine of the early arrival of a more agreeable atate of things. We have to deal with a stubborn and ignorant people, accustomed to living in the Open, and inured to the fatigues of hunting and ePort. Any serious reduction in the numerical strength of our forces would encourage the leaders We have mentioned to greater exertions., and in- duce the burghers to believe that we were weary of the struggle. The situation is thus uncertain, and by no means assuring.

After many contradictions and corrections it is tiov? reported from Paris, with an appearance of certainty, that the legacy to President Loubet is 150,000 francs. A sum of £6,000 received from an old lady—the widow of a friend in the Senate --whom he never suspected had any such design Upon him—will be welcome to this thrifty Head , the French Government. M. Loubet comes of ournble stock, and never shows any desire to con- ceal the fact ; on the contrary it has been his plea- re on may occasions to tear himself away from tLi e affairs of State to visit his mother in the little c.ountry town from which he sprung. It is notor- -I°lle that for men who desire to keep their hands 'clean politics is not a profitable pursuit, and some of the Presidents of the French Republic have left the office poorer than they entered it. M. Loubet though he has never spared the hospitalities 131 his station, will not do that. This remem- orance of him, while it might seem odd in our country, is thought in France a pretty tribute of iientirnent. It is the more appropriate because— " might be said of Lord Beaconsfield when a likinallar little event happened to him—he had not `2,enn self-seeking. Lord Beaconsfield did not like 'To lucky circumstance to be talked of, and he was tightly annoyed at the sneers cast at him in feet of of the wealth of his wife. No marriage I?,etweeo young people out of their teens could have 'con more of a love match than this. This lady W.as intensely proud of her husband, and her finan- -1 aid saved him from a great deal of anxiety. ie Statesman who arranged so astutely the pur- 'e_,[iiise of Suez Canal shares for the country, was a vtull hand at money making for himself.

div.head: War.
div.p: War.
Corrupt London Society.
His Denunciation of the War.

Sir John Brunner, Bart., M.P., for the Northwich Division, visited Davenham on Tuesday night, to return thanks for his election for the fifth time. He said that. throughout the contest he had never been able to say anything about the origin of the war. Mr Chamberlain told them in the House of Commons that President Kruger had given way on nine-tenths of the demands. At this time the English people in the Transvaal were increasing in numbers to the extent of 1,000 a week,and if Mr Chamberlain had accepted the nine tenths the Dutch people would have given way about the other tenth, and eventually would have voted cheer- fully and unanimously annexation to the British Em- pire. He had watched the proceedings and vulgarity of Mr. Chamberlain, and the Colonial Secretary's declara- tion that the concessions of President Kruger had been got out of him like water out of a squeezed sponge, de- feated its purpose,and made the Dutcn extremely angry. He had said nothing about the Raid,but be now asserted that every Jew stockbroker in London, and every big shareholder in the Cbartered Company, knew that the Raid was coming off, and unloaded their shares upan the unsuspecting Britishers. This was the sort of thing for which he (Sir John) had the profoundest contempt, and he did not like that sort of man to influence the policy of this country. (" No.") The raid took place, and Mr Cecil Rhodes was solemnly found by tee committee appointed by the Government to have deceived his col. leagues, the Governor of Cape Colony, and the Govern- ment at home. Yet, Mr. Chamberlain said in the House of Commons that Mr. Rhodes had done nothing deroga- tory to his character as an English gentleman. Whether they would ever find out why Mr. Chamberlain should I say this, after signing a report that Mr. Rhodes had lied t,.? one set of men after another, he (Sir John) did not know. Mr. Chamberlain's idea of what constituted an English gentleman was not his, and Mr. Rhodes ought Ito have been struck off the Privy Council in disgrace. How could they expect the Dutch in South Africa to believe that they were honest? From the time of the raid the Boers spent £3,000,000 in artillery' and the Government sail never a word. Knowing all this, and knowing further that every man of influence in London, and every lady of fashionable family bad been tempted with offers of shares by the speculators in South African mines, be declared that the state of London Society had been utterly corupt over this busi- ness,and they bad been all sold by the Jews (Applause.) Now they knew why he had taken the action he did, and condemned the war, and he should go on condemn- ing it. They might call him pro-Boor if they liked, but he held that those men in Johannesburg, the Extines,the Beights, the Wernhers, the Cohens, the Joel 3, the Gurtz, the Barnatos, and all the bad crew of them were not worth the bones of one gallant Cheshire boy (applause.) Had he (Sir John) been a chairman of a company dependingfor its profits upon contracts with the War Office and the Admirallty, or if ho had been up to the neck in shares, and had suited his politics to his pockets he would have been accepted by the Tories as a patriot of the purest water (applause).

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
[By a Correspondent.]

The election has been fought and won by the Liberals, and the constituency of Northwich has rapidly assumed its general business aspect, which fore, time had been "off the rail4,"whilst the virtues of Sir J T Brunner, M.P., and Mr C L Samson were being extolled. I put it that way; though,it would be more fair to say whilst the so-called vices of the Liberal candidate were being enlarged and magni— fied; and the virtues and vices of the Conservative candidate (if any existed) were being entirely ignored, in the brazen blast of Pro-Doer!

Thanks, however, to the faith and stability of 5,377 good and true Liberals, the Tory assault was of no avail, and the constituency still retains the services of one of the most respected Commoners now serving in the House ; and a gentleman who as a chairman of committees has tile confidence and trust of both sides of the House. Notwithstanding this the Conservatives pride themselves upon hav- ing gained a moral victory, and claim the adherence of a larger following than ever. To the Liberals it is naturally a matter of regret, but the lesson the election has taught, is the salutory one of "keeping the house in order," and should prove beneficial if followed up with profit. No one, however, can shut his eyes to the fact that the election has not been a political one. Rather, it has been fought on the issues of personalities ; and, as such, is an object lesson to even those who run. At the outset of the contest Sir John challenged his opponents to take the seat off him on "Political grounds "—and it is well-known none dare attempt it. Now, the constituency is additionally assured, for even a personal attack has failed. Truly, then, can the Liberals glory in an unassailable Political Candi- date, with a personality beyond reproach ; and as long as Sir John is willing to serve, he should be allowed, for no better representative could be found. He is, indeed, a representative mindful of both majority and minority, with a record that will stand the test of time.

Here we have Sir John Brunner's official message of thanks to the electors of Northwich Division. In it he says:—"Sever was a man, never was a party, better served or more stoutly supported. The con- test through which we have just gone gives much food for reflection. If, during the last twelve months I had been chairman ot a company depend- ing upon contracts with the War (Mlle, or had I been up to the neck in South African mining shares and had suited my politics to my pocket, I should have beetfiaccepted by the Tory party as a patriot of the puilast water. Being, however, a lover of peace, and having declared as I did in May last at the celebrated meeting in Liverpool, that the war might have been avoided by a wise and honest statesmanship, having been convinced, and having often declared my opinion that peace was made hopeless by the intrigues of the capitalists of the Transvaal, mainly foreigners, who wanted power in their own hands in order to secure cheap wages by substituting black labour for white, I have been denounced as an enemy to my country and a sup- porter of its enemies. In order to obtain one more vote in the HOLISB of Commons for the party which gives doles to the rich at the expense of the poor the Tories throughout the division have both before and throughout the contest circulated unfounded accusations against me as an employer; In the face of these unworthy tactics and the tremendous difficulties they have entailed upon my friends and upon me, I consider the majority cast for me last Saturday to be a real triumph."

I learn that Sir John Brunner, M.P., will on Saturday next, vi4t the Runcorn Liberal Club for the purpose of thanking the workers and members of the Club personally. The time announced is 7.30. There should be a good gathering to meet him. It is pleasing also to see that the Club has commenced to right itself, and in future the Debating Society, Social Committee, and Recreation and Literary Committee should accomplish much.

FOOTBALL. The blow Runcorn experienced at the hands and feet of Widnes on Saturday, is a very serious one to the Runcorn Club. For in addition to losing the match they had Houghton and Warders put hors de combat, and virtually by one bad stroke of luck lose their two captains. Houghton, whom 1 have seen is indeed very oad, and not likely to be fit again until Christmas or a little after. His injuries are to the collar-bone and scapular, though so far Dr. Jones has reserved his opinion as to their true ex- tent ; he does not hesitate to say that they are serious. Warder's injuries he has been able to cope with straight off, and that player can look forward to resuming his place at a much earlier date than the veteran international. As 1 say these are serious losses to the team and throw us upon the re- serve very much. Thank goodness, however, the Runcorn reserves are doughty and tough, actuated by !capital spirit, and are to be relied on. The duties of full back will be fora time entrusted to Jolley, but the other changes in the team will be regulated if anything by results. On Saturday next we have a rest so far as the first team is con- cerned, and that it comes at a welcome stage is something to feel grateful for.

THE LATE Miss CRO9FIELD.—On Suaday morning, at the Frodsham Parish Church, the Vicar, the Rev. H. B. Blogg, preached from the words " Let us not be weary in well doing." and made touching allusion to the recent loss of Miss Crosfield, who had been such a zealous and indefatigable worker for the spiritual welfare 1 of both old and young.

div.p: local and personal influences a weight which they do not possess in great and populous towns." We should think the general opinion will be that the coubties have very markedly participated in the "general sense of the nation "—a rather ambiguous phrase at the best. From our point of view and that of many others the counties have been far the saner of the two sections of the elec- torate, and have not allowed themselves to be blinded by the war fever which ran riot in the towns. The "World ", for the sake of the cause it espouses, had far better have remained silent.

We are afraid the whole literature of the elec- tion—the late election it may now be called— might be searched in vain for a really dis- tinguished phrase, a simile of the very first class, or a new idea which has ally chance of being re- membered at the contests of twenty years hence. There is an absence of invention which is almost alarming. The genius who gave us the big loaf and the little loaf has probably passed away; has he left no intellectual successors? Then, in the world of phrases," Home rule means Rome rule," a jingle which is fathered upon various speakers and writers, was excellent in its way ; and a number of similar pithy sayings of the kind will recur to anyone who recalls the events of recent contests. What legacy is there from the election of 1900? Mr. Morley's contri- bution to the polemics of the time has the finest literary flavour • but his " boastful skippers with their cargo of Dead Sea apples" has not the point and the ring, the simplicity and directness of aim which distinguish a political phrase destined to live. Again, in Mr Chamberlain's letters and mations the quotation from the Mayor of Mafe- king, which by all the laws of adaptation he has made his own is of limited application, suited only to the circumstances of the time. Then his re- ference to the legs of the caterpillar as distinguished from the wings of a bird needs a voluminous com- mentary to explain it, if it is to be detached from its context. Even Ireland has failed to give us a striking epithet, though it must be confessed Mc. Tim Healy's description of an opponent as a, " Claremorris cockroach" reaches almost distinc- tion in vituperation. Mediocrity is the hall-mark of the best of this year's electioneering, and oblivion is closer at hand than usual—an excellent thing, perhaps, for all persons concerned.

There is more encouragement for Liberals than Tories to be derived from the General Election so far as it has gone. "Joe" and his party by their unconstitutional act expected to catch the Liberals napping and at the same time take full benefit from the war-fever, and they have succeeded in both, but not to the extent expected by them- selves. It was the confident Conservative belief that they would make a clean sweep of the polls, and there must be considerable disappointment in the fact that they have only just managed to hold their own. There was no doubt about the return of the Government from the first and very little about the majority being maintained, but to find that the Opposition is con- sistently gaining a seat every time the Government wins one must be a bitter pill for the Chamberlain party to swallow. Liberalism is making a gallant fight against tremendous odds, and by the timd the election is finished the Government will fine itself face to face with a stronger and more united Opposition than at any time during the past fly e years. They had gained nothing by this "snatc h' election except a renewal of power which they did not need. In fact the short sharp fight hs:adone more to cement the ranks of Liberalism than all the agitation, argument, and diplomacy conceivable. That is why there is more encourage- ment for Liberals than Tories.

Ratepayers will be quite accustomed to being disfranchised presently, and even the ignorant among them will have a pretty good idea what such a large word means. Many were deprived of their votes by the Government at the general election, and on the Ist of November the whole of the voters in Warrington will probably be deprived of the opportunity of exercising the franchise by the action of the political leaders in the town, who for reasons best known to themselves but not entirely strange to others,have decided upon a compromise. Last November the same thing was done, and the proceedings were only enlivened by the advent of one or two independent candidates who had no chance. There is this to be said for the com- promise, that it results in men of some standing and ability being selected to fill the vacancies in the Council at very little expense. And from the point of view of those selected there is something more to be said— they obtain the honou7 cheaply. But we do not like the prinoiple of compromises, which take away a townsman's right of saying who shall re- present him on the governing body. The rate- payers themselves are much opposed to such a pro- ceeding and there are many who would vote for any independent candidate who entered the field, 'as a sort of protest against being disfranchised. We hope compromises will soon be done away with, I and that men who want to enter the Council will do so legitimately and by the desire of the majority of voters.

div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
A Provincial Letter.

Now that the General Election is over, and both sides are agreed that the three-quarters of a million sterling 18 a big sum to pay for ascertaining whether the Unionist Government should be empowered to see the South African difficulty through, there are other questions of pressing pub- lic importance which we in the provinces may fairly expect to be taken in hand, without much further delay. Perhaps the most urgent of these will be the determination of what proportion of the war indemnity the Transvaal and the Orange River Colony will have to bear, and what the British tax- payer will have to pay. The terms of settlement as regards the annexed territory will, of course, involve the expenditure of much time and con- sideration, and there will be other matters arising out of the war and of the Election. That of the lodger franchise might very well arise out of the latter. There is also the question of secondary educa- tion; and of late there has been a desire expressed that Parliament were sitting in the expectation that the coal crisis might be dealt with. The defence of the coal owners offered by the President of the South Staffordshire and East Worcestershire Institute of Mining Engineers on Tuesday convinces no one but the coal-owner. Coal prices, the public were assured, are no more than "rational," though, in his presidential address, Mr. Meacham made no mention of the very substantial dividends which some of the colliery proprietors are known to have reaped during the recent " boom " ; nor did he endeavour to reconcile with the so-called " rational" increases in the price, the fifty per cent. advance which the customer has had in many cases to meet. If this is to be accepted as a "rational " demand by the self—sacrificing coal owner, the public have little to expect from that quarter.

In France they are a little ahead of us in the matter of borrowing and lending, both of money and goods. The rate of interest there,in civil trans- actions, is fixed by law at four per cent., and in commercial matters at iive per cent. In the new civil code it is provided that, in the applications which are limited to the payment of a certain sum, the damages resulting from delay in the perform- ance shall only consist in a judgment for the in- terest allowed by law, subject to the special rules applying to commerce and to secinities. These damages are due without the creditor being obliged to show any loss ; but they are only due from the day of demand, except in the cases in which the law makes them run as a matter of right.A creditor who shall have suffered, independently of the de- lay, a loss caused by the ill-will or bad faith of the debtor, shall be entitled to obtain damages on this account, independent of the interest which became due by reason of the delay. If the borrower does not return the things borrowed or their value at the time agreed upon, he owes interest thereon from the day of the issue of the summons, or of the I demand at law.

Eleven hours a day is now the maximum number of hours that children and young people, under eighteeu, may legally work in France factories. Ilitherto,there has been a good deal of unscrupulous evasion of the French Factory Acts, but now there has begun a stricter supervision and enforcement of the law. In the English Provinces eleven hours would, of course, appear to be a long day's work,

but it is broken by one hour of rest, which may be taken at one or more periods, and two years hence the maximum is to be reduced by half an hour, and four years hence by an hour, subject to the hour's rest just mentioned.

Once again as winter approaches trouble seems brewing among the railway men. This time it is on the Great Western Railway. At a mass meet- ing on Monday the men had under consideration the following explicit demands .—" (1) A guaran- teed week to all men ; (2) eight and ten hours a day to all grades; (3) that each day stand by itself; (4) that Sunday duty be paid for independent of the week at the rate of time and ''a half; (5) that waiting orders be recognised as actual work, and paid for ; and (6) that enginemen and firemen be paid booking on and off duty, guards and brakes- men thirty minutes before train time and after arrival. For some time past there have been mur- murs of dissatisfaction from railway men, and now that Mr. R. Bell,the secretary of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants, has been returned to Parliament, it would appear that the men are look- ing to him to secure for them that which they han- ker after. Mr. Bell has more than once expressed his disapproval of strikes, and if the men are deter- mined in pressing their demands it is hoped that his efforts to bring about a conciliation of the con- flicting interests may not be in vain. A strike on the Great Western Railway might have far-reach- ing consequences, even if it did not extend to other systems, of which there would, of course, be a danger.

Both day and Sunday school conductors in cer- tain parts.of Yorkshire are greatly distressed by the spread of cigarette smoking among their scholars. There is no doubt as to the prevalence and nature of the evil, and in the public dis- cussions which have taken place on the subject, it has been suggested that there should be more severe discipline in the matter, and that no boy who smokes cigarettes should be allowed to enter a Sunday school. Boys probably do not smoke during school hours on week days and it is not easy to determine how the stricter discipline of the teachers is to be enforced. The parents seem to be the authorities in the mat- ter, and the proper persons to take it sericrusly in hand. Every right-minded person would like to see the school managers succeed, but without the assis- tance of the parents they will find it a difficult task. Certain School Boards have resolved that all tobacco found in the pockets of boys in class shall be confiscated. There are boys to be found, how- ever, who smile at the penalties and smoke on. One is reminded that there is an Act of Parliament which prohibits the sale of fireworks to children, and that it ought not to be impossible to secure the passing of an Act to prevent the sale of cigarettes or tobacco to juveniles.

Most people admire collections of rare butterflies and moths. There are those who would now like to see a few mosquitoes added, and one can speak feelingly on this point. For, in the innocency of our youth, we had fondly imagined that such a thing as a mosquito was unknown as far ar Mother England was concerned. Ignorance then ought to have been bliss. Having seen and felt it, the possi- bility of blissful ignorance no longer remains. There are mosquitoes and mosquitoes, even in Eng- land, and the best of them are a pest. Some are fairly tame, when filled with a surfeit of blood, while others are simply wild. The last are, of course, most to be dreaded. They have in some cases, perhaps, partaken of bad food; hence their sting is more poisonous. People are sometimes fond of insects. Some, like Mark Twain, are fond of fleas; but one's present knowledge of insects generally, and the mosquito in particular, is not encouraging.

div.head: immumeMm•Ms THE DANGERS OF THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: immumeMm•Ms THE DANGERS OF THE SHIP CANAL.
Death of a Sailor.

Mr:R Dpbson, coroner, held an inquest, at the Run- corn Police Court, on Wedoesdxy last, on the holy of William R Russell, first officer of the " Thornlietank," a full rigged ship, of Glasgow, who met his death by falling into the Ship Canal, on Tuesday evening. Deceased was but 25 years of age, and his sad end cuts short a very promising career:

Robert Alexander Watt, second mate of the full rigged ship " Thorniebank,",of Glasgow, said he resided at Sunny Cottage, Brottie-ferry, Seotland. The deceased was first mate of the vessel. They b3th lett the ship together between 6 and 6.30 the previous night, and spent the evening in town. The ship was lying off the lay-by. They returned to the ship at 11. o'clock the same night. When about opposit s the bows of the vessel the mate said "let us go aboard." He replied, " wait al minute the gangway lamp is a little further tois way ." He turned to the mate and just saw him fall into the Canal. Be would think that tee mate got his foot into a small water-course and that caused him to stumble over the wall. As the mate fell he tried to grasp him and only just toweled his arm Be hailed the mate, but got no answer. He then went on board and aroused the Captain and another man on board; and he himself was lowered to the water's edge, but could not see the deceased. There were no lights on the wharf only the Ship's lights. With the assistance, of a boats-crew from another ship the bodywas recovered —By Inspector Hicks. He thought that if the dock had been lighted better the accident would not have occured He had been at sea for many years bet was never in a II worse lighted port in his life. James Mcßride. the captain of the " Tnornliebank," said the deceased was the first officer of the ship. His name was William R. Russell, and he lived at the Queen's Ferry Arms Hotel, South Queen's Ferry, Scot- land. He was about 25 years of age and single. They ; had sailed together for the past four years, and deceased was always very steady. He corroborated the first witness with regard to the attempt to rescue the deceased, but it was not until three quarters of an hour afterwards that the body was recovered. It was a very dark night, and there were no lights on the quay. If there had been light; there, the accident would never I have happened.—try Inspector Hicks: He considered Ithat the condition of the port was such in re earl to lights that he was justified in_saying it was the most dangerous place he had been in. Sergeant Samuel Gregory swore he examined the body Taere was a small scar on the right side of the nose probably the result of grappling. His neck was very discoloured and blood was oozing from the right ear. The captain recilled said that when the body was breught on deck there was blood oozing out of one ear, and as it was slightly warm, he tried to restore the body bv artificial respiration. which WAS kept up for an hour and a half. He also wishei to take tne opp3Aunity of thanking the Missioner (Mr. Seaw) and 'he people of the Mersey Mission for the trouble and kindness that had been extended to bine in taking in the body of one whom he well liked. The deceased was a good swimmsr and the fact that he was never again seen after falling into the water probably indicated that no had been stunned by the fall. After a brief deliberation the jury returned a verdict of " Found Drown,d," and recommended that the Ship Canal Authorities should be approached with the view of getting the place provided with better lightiae. Mr. Dicev, who was preeent,said that he would con- vey the recommendation of the jury to the Company.

div.head: BOATWOIVIAN'S SAD END.
div.p: A BOATWOIVIAN'S SAD END.

The Runcorn Police Court was the scene of another in- quest, on Wedneslay morraing, when Coroner R D 'neon, presided over a jury, of which Nlr Winfield,wls the fore- man, impannelled for the purpose of investigatio!r, the caut;e of the death of Mrs Sopnia Brown, whose body was found floatinz in the ship canal on 'Monday.

George Brown, 20, Norfolk-street, Runcorn, a flatman disposed to being in charge of the flat "Thompson." The body viewed by the jury was that of his wife Sophia, aged 56 years. Oa Saturday, the 6th lust, th, flat was lying in the Ship Canal. He gave his wife 7s 61 to go ashore to buy supplies, and she returned about 1 o'clock after being away for a little more than an hour. she left the boat again saying she was going to the loft, but he did not see her again. Amy Hignett. wife :sf William Hignett, 12, Norton- street, stated she knew the :deceased. She last saw her about three o'clock coming oul., 'if Vie Derby Arms. She said they would not fill her anything at the Derby Arms as they said she was drunk. Witness a ivised her to go to her daughters, but she went towards the Ship Canal. Jeseph Kirkham, of Randle Sluicls, said he found the body of the deceased on the 16th just, in the Ship Canal between the Quarry Hole and Norton Brook outfall. He secured the body with a rope and placed it beyond rnich of pasing steamers. Sabsequently he assisted P.C. Upton to get the body out of the canal. P.C. Upton corroborated. Be had also examined the body and found that part of the mouth and cheek had been eaten away by rats. The body was fully clothed but there was no property upon it. The jury returned a verdict of found drowned.

Lymm people will sympathize with Mr. Roger Gaddum, of Westview, Lymm, and with Mr. Theo- dore Gaddum, of Massey Hall, Thelwall, on the sudden death of Mr. Roger Gaddum's brother, who was found dead by the roadside at Wilmslow on Sunday evening. div.head: SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES.

Mrs. Elizabeth Holt, a widow, who resided at 34, Peethouse-lane, Widnes, died suddenly on Saturday afternoon. About 3 p.m. she was seen a; the front door shaking hands with one of her sons, who was going to a convalescent home at Wootton. She then went into the house, and tell asleep in a chair in the kitchen. About 3.45 Jane Lghtfoot, a grand- daughter of deceased, who was in the house, noticed something wrong with her grandmother, and called in her uncle, and a neighbour. The doctor was sent for, but the woman expired a few minutes before his arrival, presumably in a fit. The Coroner has intimated he does not think an inquest necessary. DEATH OF MR REGINA.LD BRUNDRIT. Mr Reginald Ernest Barclay Brundrit, eldest son of the late Mr John Brundrit of The Highlands, !Runcorn, died on Wednesday morning at tce early age of 27 years. The news reached Runcorn by telegraph and created a feeling of profound regret amongst those who had the privilege of being acquainted with the family. He had been ailing Ifor some time. The deceased gentleman had evinced an interest in volunteer matters and for "several years he was Captain of the F Company of the 2nd Cheshire V.B. regiment, stationed at Run- corn. He resigned his commission in June last. He was one of.the patriotic ;band of Volunteers who offered themselves for the front in South Africa, but unfortunately he failed to pass the medical examination. Two younger brothers survive him.

div.head: LATE MR. MARSHALL, OF WIDNES.
div.p: THE LATE MR. MARSHALL, OF WIDNES.

A special servicJ in memory of the late Mr. Wil- liam Marshall was held in the Gospel Union Mis- sion, West Bank, Widnes, on Sunday last. There was a crowded congregation. The choir, under the conductorship oc Mr T Bowen, rendered appropriate hymns and the anthem, "Vital Spark," Miss Bowen the Swansea and Bagillt Eisteddfods premier prize winner, renderel with remarkably tine effect" Re shall feed his fbck " (Messiah "). The preacher, Mr. Minor, the evangelist, selected his text from Proverbs xiv., If a man die, shall he live again?" and H. Corinthians v. 1, " We know if the earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, a house not made by hands, eternal in he heavens." Reference was made by the preacher to the late Mr Marshall's 14 years' con- nection with this mission, during which time he had held the position of superintendent of the Sunday school. leader of the Choir, and treasurer. The ser- vice was very impressive. Much sympathy was evinced by the cmgregation with the widow and the relatives, who were largely in attendance.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
St. Edward's Catholic Church, Runcorn.

Last Sunday the annual sermons in cenneetion with the patronal festival were preached by the riev. Father Aloysius, C.P., St. Anne's Retreat, Sutton. At the morning service the preacher took for his text the words of St. Luke i. 7, and in the course of his remarks he said the story of the human race was a strange one. Historians and learned men divided it into t vo periods, that of the world before and that of the world since the cross. Both were like one another in some respeets and were very unlike in other respects. In each were the same tale of man's petty ambitions, his loves, and his hates. When they came to examine the last two thou- sand years and compare them with the last two theusands years before the cross they found a great difference. Toe pages of pagan history showed that the soldier was left on the battle field with no one to staunch the wounds from which his life's blood ebbed away. They also read that woman was the slave of man, the little children were regarded as a bar to human progress, ' and the blind, deaf, and afflicted ones were driven to despair and suicide. They could see to what depths of degradation humanity had fallen. In reading the pages that related the doings of the last thousand years they could perceive the marvellous crtange. 'foe soldier was no longer left on the battlefield to die of want. There were with him willing hands and loving hearts to make his last hours peaceful. Woman, toe, had been raised to the pedestal intended for her ; pubic opinion snatched the little ones from ttie hands of rile parents, and there was special hom-s set apart, for the blind, de if and afflicted. To whom and to what did they owe this change ? The answer was Jesus Christ and Christianity. Christianity V 7,1•1 a fact and Jesus Cnrist was the centre. Who then was Jesus Christ ? lie was the eternal answer to the appeal of humanity. Religion was the passion of the human race. Whether they read the Grecian philosophers or the histories of primeval savages they could see the longing of the heart of man to kaow something of the great wonder that existed. His heart told him there must be sonaeone greater than himself. The universe, with its mysteries, its wondrous order, and its variety, pro- claimed to his intelligence the existence of some won- drous being. The human heart appealed for something that would bring that groat eternal being near to him. So the Eternal Father sent down his only Son, who was the keynote, the history of the world's hopes and desires. The musical portion of the service was performed by a band and chorus of over forty members. Signs of care- ful rehearsal were visible in every one of the musical items. The "Messe des Anges" was brilliantly executed, while "Ad te Levavi" received meritorious treatment. At the evening service his text was, "Behold all genera- tions shall call me blessed," and he dealt with the imma- culate conception of Mary the Mother of God. The fol- lowing compositions of the late S. Moorat were given with excellent harm my and precision by the Runcorn Orchestral Society (leader Mr II Handley), and members of the choir. "Erculter, Omnium Turba," "Ave Maria" No 4, "Salve Regina" No 4, "0 Salutaris" No 24, "Ave Verum" No 2, "Tantum Ergo" No 5, "Et Vitam Venturi" ("Messe des Anges''), Mr P I Bate, Warrington, wielded the baton in a very capable manner, and sensibly in- fluenced the musical portion of the service. The collec- tions, in aid f the sehools, were very satisfactory. There were large congregations at bath services, in spite of the inclement weather.

div.head: NORTHWICH DIVISION ELECTION.
div.p: NORTHWICH DIVISION ELECTION.
Liberalism Triumphs Over
Khaki.
Sir J. T. Brunner Returned.

One of the most notable elections in the annals of the Nortnwich Parliamentary Division was brought to a conclusion on Saturday. Sir John T. Brunner. Bart., who has represented the constituency in four Parlia• meats, for the sixth occasion championed the cause of Liberalism. His opponent was Mr. Charles Leopold Samson, solicitor, ot Manchester, Conservative: For Mr. Samson "khaki" was tho only wear. At the out- set he declared Sir John to be a " pro-Boer "and "little Englander" which he sought to prove by the weak method of narrating the meetings the worthy Baronet had attended in regard ts the South African question where opinions opposed to those of the Government of the day had been expressed. This he reiterated ad nauseant. Even his own supporters became wearied of the one topic, and attempts to drag from him some declaration of political faith by means of questions failed, fur of political history and political questions be seemed to have a lamentable lack of knowledge. His supporters, however, had found other means of trying to Oust Sir John from his seat. To them politics were of no moment, ad the administration of the works of Messrs. Brunner, Mond and Co. was assailed with a view, if possible, of blacking Sir John's character. It was alleged that men over 30 years of age were not taken on at the works, and the base calumny found wide acceptance, and at one time imperilled Sir Joho's chances of success. By the workmen themselves and the secretary of the Company the statement was proved to be false, but Sir John had to give the allegation the lie direct, before hundreds of the working people were convinced. In his speeches Sir John showed himself to be the sound Radi- cal politician he ever was, with large views of England's Imperial destiny, and as the election progressed the nrighter becam 3 the chances of retaining his seat, and on Saturday last, the polling day, Sir John and his sup- porters were confident of success, with a diminished majority. The constituency was flooded with literature of all kinds, and the walls were one patchwork of blue and red posters, of assertion and contradiction, while both parties vied with each other in arranging meetings. The Liberals too went in for open-air gatherings in advo- cating their cause, and in this highly successful depart- ment, great credit is due to Mr. McHugh, Mr. loose, and Mr. I. 0. Williams. It must be admitted, however, that the organisation of the Liberal party in Runcorn was not equal to that of past years, due to a variety of causes. Many old workers held aloof, but new recruits were forthcoming, and a number of ladies rendered sr- vices which deserve due acknowledgment. Ever assiduous too were Mr. S. Taylor, J.P., chairman of Runcorn North, and Mr. A. R. Norman, J.P.. chairman. of Runcorn South, who sought to inTire their followers with their own enthusisam.

The polling stations for the other districts were as follows :—lston-by-Sat- ton, Board School ; Barnton, the Church Schools ; Day- enham, the National Schools ; Halton, the Parochial School; Marston, the Now Church Schools; Middlewich, the National Schools (2) ; Runcorn (North), National Schools (4) ; Runcorn (South), Board Schools (2) ; weaverham, the Board School ; and Weston, the Catho- lic School. William Peers, Harry Barnton ; Runcorn South, 1, William John Ford, J F Moulton; Runcrn, South, 2, El LW Mullard.Francis Digging; Weaverhatn, Henry John Ford, J J S Harper ; Weston, El L H Millard, D Walker; Viiinnington, J Ei Cooke, William Hodge ; Winsford, Over, Rob.rt H Jack- son, James Merrimon ; VVinsford,Over,H C 0 Pritchard, E J Jones ; Winsford Wharton, NV H Eige, G Booth. The general arrangements were carried out by Mr. Cullimore, acting', under sheriff, and Mr J Higgins, who is well experienced in the duties. In the various districts the Liberal sub-agents were— Barnton, W C Deakin ; Davenham, George Shaw; Halton, F W Johnson ; Marston, W C Deakin ; Middle- wich, J C Powell : Northwich (Castle), George E King; Northwich (Leftwich and Witton), J J Dixon; Runcorn (North), Clement Handley ; Runcorn (South), Fred Whalley ; Weaverham, Albert E Gatley ; Weston, Thomas Leech ; Winnington,NVilliam Janion ; Winsford (Over), NV H Tolfree ; Winsford (Wharton), Joseph Newall.

For the Conservative party the sub-agents were— Barnton, R L Fryer; Daveriham, M Earlaaa ; Marston. Jsmes Renshaw ; Middlewich, F B Aley Cooke; North- wich (Castle), Hugh Adderley ; Northwich (Leftwich). Frank Les ; Northwich (Witton), George A Hughes ; Runcorn (North), T Fl Annett ; Runcorn (South) and Weston, William Eiward Lancaster ; Weaverham, Harry Halamshaw Hughes; Winnington, James Archi- bald Douglas ; Winsford (Over), Joseph Parkinson; Winsford (Wharton), William Shaw. At Runcorn the party agents and workers were early astir, and soon after the poll opened a large number of vehicles were en evidence, bringing up voters to the polling station.. These were situated at the National Schools, Churcli•street, and at the Victoria-road Board Schools. Runcorn represents an important portion of the constituency, the register nn which the election was taken showing no less than 2.911 voters, divided thug:— Runcorn North Electoral Division, 1,972 ; Runcorn South, 939. Tte supporters of the respective parties were most indefatigable in their interests, and it is cor- rect to say that never before has a contest been waged with greater vigour and determination by both sides. Toe party colours—red for the Conservatives and Unionists, and blue and yellow for the Liberals—were made the most of, many of the vehicl being gaily decorated, while officials and supporters of both candidates wore miniature portraits of their favourites decorated with rosettes. Many of the Liberals sported yellow flowers in preference to the regulation ribbon. The weather was of the most unfavourable character. Rain fell intermittently throughout the whole day, and the air was raw and cold, rendering the task of the respective party workers anything but an easy and agreeable one. This, notwithstanding, both sides worked most indefatigably, and inquiry at the polling stations shortly nefore the poll closed elicited the fact that there had been heavy voting. The outside of the stations presented an unusually animatel appearance, the roadway being thronged with men and women be- ing anxious to see the finish. It was pleasing to note, howev,r,that everything passed off without disturbance, and that while each side occasionally called for cheers for their respective favourite, nothing of a disagreeable character arose which required the intervention of the p )fice. During the day the two gentlemen contesting the seat visited the town and were accorded a hearty reception from their supporters. After the poll had closed the ballot boxes were taken by conveyance to Northwich.

Immediately after the poll was closed the boxes were sealed, and conveyed from the respective polling booths to the Northwich Police Station, the last to arrive being those from Runcorn. They were then paced in one of the cells, the door of which was sealed.

div.head: Counting.
div.p: The Counting.

Oa Monday nnrning, undor the supervisiln of Mr. Cnllimore and Mr. Higgins, the ballot boxei were re- moved from the Nortbwich Police Station to the Verdin Technical Schools, where the counting was commenced at 10-30, and conducted with the utmost expedition, in the presence of tho candidates and several of their chief supporters. It was not, however, until one o'clock had struck that the High Sheriff, Mr. Roberts, came to the
door and announced th 3 result to the vast crowd which had congregated. The figures were : Brunner Samson 4,678
Majority

I It will thus be taea that ot those on the register 10,055 exercisad the franchise, thus leaving nearly 2,000 voters who had failed to present themselves before the Presiding Officers at the various booths throughout the division. There were eight spoiled votes. Oa the proposition of Sir John Brunner, seconded by Mr. Samson, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the High Sheriff and his officials, for the able manner in which they had conducted their assiduous labours.

The declaration of the result at Runcorn evoked a great outburst of enthusiasm and at the Liberal Club the flag was immediately hoisted amid tremendous cheer- ing at 5.30. Tae newly elected member accompanied by Lady Brunner arrived at Runcorn station from Nprtbwich and received a splendid greeting. They were at once driven to the residence of Mr S Taylor, where they partook of tea. In the meantime BAhesda Lecture Hall had been engaged and at half-past six it was crowded with an audience throbbing with excitement and enthusiasm which found vent in the singing of s:mgs composed by Mr W Handley in honour of the victory. _ _ _ _ _

When Sir John and La ly Brunner entered the room the audience rose eit masse wildly cheering and waving hats and handkerchiefs and it was some minutes before Mr Taylor who took the chair could commence the pro- ceedings. On the platform were Sir John and Lady Brunner, Messrs A R Norman, J R Frith, James Lea, T Lea, W Handley, H W Handley, C Handley,G Bellamy,; M Frith, W C Cooke, W Handley, and others. Prior to , the commencement of the meeting the audience joined , in singing" Where is now the mighty Samson? "to the tune of Soldiers of the Queen," " Sir John is still our member," and " ALIA Lang Syne." Mr S Taylor, who was recetved with ringing cheers, said it gave him extreme pleasure to introduce to them Sir John Brunner as their representative. (Applause.) He could assure them they were all disappointed when they heard the result of the poll. ies they knew, five years ago Sir John was returned by a majority of over 1,600, and that day his majority was about 700. That was the result of slander and all sorts of jobs by their opponents. (Hear, hear.) They must put their house in order. They were very much to blame for their lack of organiz ttion. If they had kept their organization up during the last five years they would not be in the position in which they found them- selves to-day. They ought to have kept up the majerity to 1,600. Most of them would feel annoyed and disap- pointed, and he took that opportunity of encouraging them to put their house in order in the matter of organ- ization. If they did that he had no fear as to the re- sult in the future. (A Voice : " 2,090 next time" and applause.) Sir John Brunner, who was received with an ovation, said Mr. Taylor had spoken to them of the great pleasure he feit in introducing him, not for the first and not for tee last thne—(hear, hear)—es their representative. Mr Taylor's pleasure did not equal his in acknowledging as he did now the gallant service Mr Taylor hid rendered for the Liberal cause during that election. (Applause.) When he went to the Licoral Cub three weeks ago he had to begin by denying that infeinous story about Branner, Mond and Co. and the 30-year-old workmen question. Teat was an awful dead weight for him and his supporters to lift, and in the face of that story to win by, 699 was a most splendid victory. (Applause). He asked Mr. Taylor to cast aside that feeling of disappointment. (A Voice : "We are not disappointed.") When he got beck to the House of Commons his vote would be just as good as Mr. Tomkinson's, who had a majority of 500 more than he had. His (Sir John's) vote would always be given steadily in the same direction. He regretted that the organization had been allowed to lapse into dis- use. Be regretted it extremely, for he was the man who taught this constituency its Liberal politics. From February to the end of November, 1885, he preached the whole gespel of Liberal p Aides, and a very large pro- portion of the men of that constituency bad hardly con- sidered politics before. Now why should not they do that again? Ought they not to study once more the grand old story of the fight of the Liberals against the Tories in favour of the liberties and prosperity of the people? Never should that duty be neglected. He was delighted to hear that a number of young men in Run- corn had determined amongst themselves that they would study how wealth was produced and how wealth was distributed in:this country. No man who ever Welled that question would ever Ise a Tory. He asked those who had not heard of this project to join themselves together in order that they might study the, first principles of Liberal politics. (Hear, hear.) He gave credit to the whole of the Liberal workers. There was not one of them—not even those wbe hesitated are() whom be had seen over and over again—there was not one man in 'the end who did not come round t 3 his side and fight for the Liberal cause. Two others he wished to give credit to. There had been two bravo and gracious ladies engaged—one was his wife and the other Mrs Samson. ( Ipplause and laughter.) If they had seen the kindly gracious way in which Mrs Samson shook hands with him and congratulated him, and also sent a message of congratulation to Lady Brunner, they would have been as pleased and delighted as he was. He cot- gratulated Mr Samson upon having such a wite. (Laugh- ter and applause.) Be had been told that in Runcorn the clergy of the Established Church had been extremely active in their :opposition to him. They all knew that he held the opinion that where public money went there should follow public control, and seeing that the voluntary schools of this country were almost en- tirely maintained by public money, he thought public management should follow. He did not advocate the teaching of the Protestant children by Catholic teachers, or Catholic children by Protestant teachers. They knew his motto—fair play all round. He would ask every Churchman and every Catholic to consider v. hat he said, and to believe that in this matter he was for fair play all round, and desired t do unto others as he would they should do unto him. (Applause). He wished to thank them again and again, and to tell them that he con- sidered this a victory ia no sense for the Tory party. Mr Samson had declared that it was a moral victory. If it had only been a moral contest he (Sir John) would have been better pleased. (Applause.) During the cort- test he had found how good-humoured the people amongst whom be lived were. There had been plen;y of booing, and that reminded him that they had beaten the booers at that election. (Laughter ) It was only the Tories who had been booine, and they had beaten the booers. (Renewed laughter.) He was delighted t'o find himself the representative of so thoroughly a good- humoured and friend:y population as they were in that division. There were 10,063 men who came to vote, and 10,055 gave absolutely correct votes. Only eight papers out of the 10,063 were spoiled. (Hear, hear.) He believed that that was the best record that had ever been known in a Parliamentary election of such magnitude, and he was proud to be the representative of a people so intelligent that they cast their votes more clearly and more satis- factorily to the Returning Officer than any set of men in the country. They knew how steadily that division bad progressed in the matter of education. Probably a good many of them knew that the county of Chester paid in technical instruction rate one-fifth of what was paid by the whole of England, and the division ref North- wich paid an enormous proportion of that ono-fifth. He (Sir John) had fought this question out at the meeting of the Union of Lancashire and Cheshire Institutes, and when men from Lancashire load boasted—especially the Chairman of the Technical Instruction Committee of the Lancashire County Council—when:they ha I boasted that this anti that town had voted a halfpenny in the L, and a farthing in the £ he the speaker) had told him that every town in the Northwich Division had voted the whole penny in the L. So might it be, and so might it continue. Might they rise in culture, rise in refinement. rise in comfort, and rise ,in brotherly love towards one another, then would they be prouder and more self-ref- peeing, and he prouder and prouder of them. (Loud applause.) Sir John, Lady Brunner, Mr. • Samuel Taylor, and others then left amid a demonstration of applause for the railway station. Here Sir John and Lady Brunner entrained for Winsford to meet the Liberal supporters and workers in that town. The large room at the Liberal Club was also filled to overflowing and the people were greatly disappointed when it became known that Sir John bad been unable to pay the club a visit and give them a greeting.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
ALLEGED THEFT OF TROWELS AT NEWTON.

At the Wsrrington Occasional Court. yesterday morn- ing before Mr F A. Frost, Mary Elizabeth Cross was charged with stealing two bricklayer's trowels, value 5s the property of Thomas Hiles, 43, Sankey-street, Earles- town, some time between six pan. on the 2nd inst and six a.m. on the 3rd inst.—Thomas Hiles stated that on Tuesday the Pod inst he was working in some houses in Cross-lane and at six p.m. he put the trowels in a bass in a shed. He left the premises and on going to work at six o'clock the folbwing morning he missed the trowels and gave information to the police.—P.C.Alfred Seddon, starioned at Lewton,said he apprehended the prisoner at 8.30 p.m. on the 3rd inst. in the Blue Bell Hotel, New- ton, where she was offering the trowels produced for sale. Be took her to Newton Police station and subse- quently charged her with the theft, and she replied. told von I took them."—Prisoner was zommitted for trial at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions. SELLING A HANDCART TWICE.

John Whittaker, 11, Naylor-street. was brought be- fore the magistrates at the Warrington Police Court on Monday. on a charge of stealing by means of a trick the sum of 18s, from James Delocze on Tuesday afternoon— Superintendent Monaghan said that the prisoner up to two month; ago worked es an out-door porter at Bank Quay Station and had a handcart. On the 27th of May he sold the handcart to a man named Ralph Nor man. Lest Tuesday he met the prosecutor, Delooze in the vaults at the Central Hotel. He had a conversation with him about the handcart, and eventu- ally agreed to sell it to him for 18', telling him that it was at Bank Quay Station. Delocze paid him the money, for which he received a receipt. but on going to the station feund the handcart had been sold in May to Norrnen. Dllooze made a search for the prisoner, and found he had absconded with the money. He did not return to Warrington until Sunday night.—Prisoner was committed to gaol for two months with hard labour, A SHOP ASSISTANT'S NEGLIGENCE AND ITS BE,IILT. At the Borough Police Court on Monday, before Mr. F Monks and other magistrates. Messrs. Povey and Duckworth, provision dealers, ButtermarkeLst., were summoned for selling margarine on the 11th ult. and -segleeting to have it wrapped in paper marked with the word margarine in half inch letters.—lnspector Norman prosecuted on behalf of the Corporation.---Mr. Browne appeared for the defendants.—Elizabeth Parker, a little girl, said that acting upon instructions from Inspector Norman she went into the shop of the defendants on the 11th ult., and asked to be supplied with a pound of ten- penny taitter. It was supplied to her in a plain wrapper and she handed it to the Inspector.—Croal.examined : She asked at first for half a pound of coffee, and was told that it was mixed with chicery. She was supplied with the other article from a dish marked margarine.— Inspector Norman said that on receiving the parcel from the last witness be went into the shop and had the shop assistant who had supplied it pointed out to him. He asked him from where he had taken the margarine, and be turned the dish marked margarine round. There were scores of wrappers marked margarine in the shop. Be asked the assistant why he had not used one and he made no answer.—Mr. Browne said the Act provided that where it was proved that an employer had no 1 knowledge of the offence, and it was committed without his connivance sr consent, the emploe 6 should be con- victed, and the employer exernted from any penaty. This margarine had been supplied, as it was, contrary to orders, and through the sheer negligence of the assis- tant. Mr. Povey, who managed the indoor department of the business, was away at the time. He had warned all his employe; not to sell margarine without it was wrapped in a proper paper. It was a partaif the duty of a shop assistant to know the provisiclif of the Act clearly.—John Smith, the shop assistant, was then charged with selling the margarine as stated, without his employer's knowledge, consent or connivance.— Mr. Povey stated that he had been in the provision trade for a great number of years. He was at Liverpool on the day in question. Defendant had been in his employ for three years. He had told him specially about the wrapping of the margarine, When he die- covered what he had done he would have discharged him but fnr Mr. Browne's advice. He had no knowledge of the offeaceeat the time,neither did he conniven or conse3t to h.—Witham %Varhurton. an assistant in the shop, said he and the others had been warned to be careful in this matter. Mr. Povey was most particular, and after he had left the shop sometimes wou'd turn back to remind them.—Defendant—admitted the offence. He denied that he turned the dish round when Mr. Norman came into the shop.—The Chairman said the case against Messrs. Povev and Duckworth would be dismissed, The assistant Smith had been guilty of gross carelessness, and would be fined 15s. The magistrates hoped that this would be a lesson to him. THE BENEFIT OF A DOI7BT. _ _

At Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday before Mr Geotge Comber and Mr J Ball, two Irishmen named John Fallen (farm labourer) and James Furey (road repairer) were charged with assaulting James Parsonage on the fib Oatober at Dam-lane,Rixton. There was also a cross-summons charging Parsonage with assaulting John Falion. Mr Browne represented Par- sonage and Mr Jonkirs appeared for Fallon and Purer.— The facts as stated by Mr Browne were to the effect that on the date named Parsonage and his younger brother were proceeding home from the wakes at Hollins Green and when about 200 yards down Dam- lane, Parsonage was accosted by Fallon, who without any provocation threw him to the ground. Whilst lying there it was alleged that Furey came up and took a running kick at Parsonage with the result that a serious wound was inflicted. Parsonage went to a cn,ctor who found a wound on the head two inches long and penetrating ta the bone. His condition was so serious that at Newton Petty Sessions a remand was granted. It wa only since the warrant was granted th.t a cross-summons was taken out against Parsonage charging him with assault. Mr. Browne's statement was borne out by Parsonage and his brother. P. C. Carke stated that when he charged Fallon with the offence, ho replied that Parsonage called him an Irish pig and almo-t choked him.—Mr. Jenkins said the de- fence was that Parsonage, wiles was under the influence of drink,was the aggressor. He used the language stated by the constable and then seized Fallon by the throat and also scratched his face. In self defence, Fallon knocked Parsonage to the ground. With regard to the charge against Furey it was a case of mistaken identity. He(Mr. Jenkins) would be able to prove by a number of witnesses that Furey was not with Fallon at the time. Fallon was accompanied by. his brother and a man named Dunne. Ile (Mr. Jenkins) had summoned Dunne to appear as a witneEs, but that individual had made good his escape to Ireland, and he would leave the magistrates to form their own cocain- sions.—A number of Irishmen were then called, who stated that whilst standing outside the Black Swan Inn, in cornpiny with Furey, a man came up and told them that there was a row in Damilano. They went there
THE MOST NUTRITiOUS.

and ascertained that a man named Parsonage had been amulted. Parsonage was not there when Furey arrived nn the scene.—Tne wagistrates decided to fine Fallon 201 end costs (including the advocate's fee), and in regard to Furey, the magistrates said there was a doubt in the ease, and they had decided to give him the benefit of it. He would be dismissed, and the charge against Parsonage was also dismissed.
GRATEFUL-CON!FORTING.
aREAKFAST AND SUPPER.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
Warrington Borough Court.
Motrnex.—Before Mr. F. Monks (in the chair). Alderman Heaton. and Messrs. Birchall, Hayward, Wright, and
Thornton

A FRUITERER FINED.--Bdwarl Oxley. fruiterer, 287, Knutsford-road. was summoned for causiig an obstruction In Bridge-street by allowing a handcart to remain there longer than was necessary for its loading or unloading.— P.C. Dyson statel that the defendant sold fruit from a handcart. •On the Bth inst the handcart stood in Bridge- street for three quarters of an hour. Defendant had been Previously warned.—Defendant said he was waiting for his brother who had gone to bring his dinner.—He was lined ss. •

YOUTHFUL GAMBLER. —Jahn Dickinson (14), 13, Brook- street; John Spilshury. (15), 43. Greenall-street ; Charles Brown (12). 94 Hiles•',ere-street ; and James Wrench (15). 19, Gilbert-street were summoned for playing " banker" in Ellesmere-street on Sunday week —P.C. Clough said defendants were playing for cigarettes.—Dickinson, who, the Chairman said, was the ringleader, was fined 7s 6d and the others 5s each,

THE FIRENVoRICS NUTSANCE.—John Cooper (13), 95, Welifield-street : John Yarweod (14). 8. Garibaldi-street ; and Arthur Jones (15), 41, Fox-street, Were summoned for setting off fireworks to the danger and annoyance of people in Green-greet on the Bth Inst.—P.C. Woods said the lads threw their fireworks into shops, and caused a great deal of annoyance.—Defendants were fined 2s Rd each. THROWING SToNES.—John Chadwick (9+, 13. Williamson's- square ; Joseph Hopwood (II), 13, Dakin's-yard ; and Robert Hill (10). 6.Dakires-yard. were ordered to be confined in the cells until six o'clock for throwing 'tones in Jackson's- entry on the 7th inst. THESDAY.—Before Mr. T. Birohall (in the chair), Alderman Hutchinson, Councillor Shaw Green and Dr. Fox. Two MONTHS FOR FAMILY NEGLECIT.—James William Davies was charged with running away from the borough and leaving his wife and five children chargeable to the Guar- dians.—Mr. B Shearer stated that the prisoner left Warring- ton in February. but his wife managed to maintain herself and family until September, when she became ill. The family had since been chargeable to the Guardians. When in town the prisoner worked for the Corporation, but he said his wages were not sufficient, and left Warrington to seek fresh employment. He wrote to his wife to say that he would send her some money, but she never received anything from him. The man had heel in the habit of neglecting his family for a long time past, and never gave his wife more than 1"s a week. He had just come out of gaol, where he had been serving a term of imprisonment for theft. Prisoner was committed to gaol'for two months with hard labour. WIFE ASSAULT—SEPARATIoN ORDER GRANTED.—Edward Hart, 13)W:oak-street. was summoned for assaulting his wife, Annie Hart on the 13th and 14th inst.—Complainant stated that on Saturday night her kusband accused her of improper conduct and illused her shamefully. On Sunday ha renewed his conduct and violently assaulted her,discolouring her face. Prisoner was drunk when be committed the assault,—The magistrates convicted the prisoner of an aggravated assault and sent him to prison for a month with hard labour. His wife was granted a separation order with 10s. a week. SLEEPING OlTT.—Charles Reynolds, of no settled abode. WAS charged with sleeping in a stable in Factory-lane about 12.45 that morning and d ,iag damage to some hay In the stable to the amount of Zip—Sergeant Smith found the prisoner in Mr. Aspinall's stable in Factory-lane. He was lying on a quantity of hay. which he had completely spoiled. He had ninepence upon him and apparently would rather damage other people's protnrty than pay for a night's lodg- ings.—Prisoner was committed for seven days.
OBSCENE LANGUAGE —For using obscene language, Catherine Longshaw. Pocket-street, was fined 53.—P.0. Carbett proved the case.
Warrington County Petty Sessions. WEDNEspsr.—Before Messrs G Comber (in the chair) and J Ball. _
.„..._... DRivING Wrrworr RElN3.—William Duffy was fined 28 6d for driving his two horses and a lurry at Itixton without reins.

THEFT OF MONEY AT HATDOCA.—John Meekan, a young Irishman who had only been in this country five weeks. was charged with stealing 15e in money from the dwelling-house of Alice Dukes, at Havelock, between the 14th and 15th October. He pleaded guilty.—Alice Dukes, Station-road, Haydock, said, that the prisoner had lodged at her house. Last Monday morning she missed the money from a drawer in the kitchen. Suspicion fell on the prisoner who had seen where the money was placed.—P.C. Thompson. of Hayclock, said he apprehended the prisoner at Lime-street Station, Liverpool, He had already taken a ticket for Foxford. County Mayo. via Holyhead. When charged he said. " I'll tell the truth. I ill titre it."—k friend of the prisoner's stepped forw trd,'and in answer to the Chairman promised to see that the boy was sent to his parents.—Prlsoner was bound over to come up for judgment whet called upon.

div.head: Runcorn Petty Sessions.
div.p: Runcorn Petty Sessions.
MONDAY. —Before Mr Charles Wynolds (La the chair) and Mr
John Octtieston.

SCHOOL BOARD DiSES : —A WARNING TO FUTURE DEFAULTERS —The following parents were each fined ss. including costs for neglecting to send their children regularly to school :---Richard Done, Cartwright-street : William Bills, Mill-brow, (two cases) : John Baz!ey. Mill-brow. (two Cases); John Monaghan, Cross-street Bernard Flannigan, Cooper-street; Jokn Limb. Loch-street, John Draper, Oakmere-street : George Morrison. Shaw-street; Sarah Lea, Gilbert-street, Peter Knight, Mill-street ; William Cooke, Union-street ; Emma Waterson Bridgewater- street ; John Harding, Shaw-street ; William Cavanagh, Gilbert - street ; Thomas WOOlgEr, Princess - street ; James Moores, Brick Kiln Houses; and James Wylde, Brick Kiln Henses.—The Chairman (Ifr Reynolds). before giving: the decision of the Bench, said If thee had chosen to act as severely as they mieht have done. they could have fined all the defendsnts £1 each. Hitherto the maximum fine had been ss. They wanted to deal as leniently as possible with the offenders until the School Board had altered their by-laws, but they must understand that if children did not make attendance to the satisfaction of the School Board their parents might he fined a sovereion instead of 53 as heretofore. The Rducation Department had deter- mined that the schools should not suffer by the careless attendance of children whose parents did not look after them. Other psrents got their children to school and they (the present defendants) would have to do the same. ALLEGED THEFT OF OLoTHING. —CHARG IC AGAINST MoTHEß.—Lavinia Dillon, aged 13, Was charged with stealing four pairs of drawers, value 3s 63. the goods of Harriet Do id. at Runcorn, on the 9th October; and further with stealing three aprons. value 2s nd, the goods of Rachael Teeter. on the 6th Octoer.—Martlea Annie Dillon, mother of the girl, was charged with receiving the four pairs of drawers, and the three aprons from her daughter, well knowing them to have been stolen. —Superintendent Pearson said Mrs Tasker was away at Manchester and he asked for a remand until Saturday next. —Sergeant Gregory stated that on Wed- nesday. the 10th October, he received the aprons from Thomas Brown He made Inquiries at all the drapers' shops In Runcorn, but failed to get them identified. He then Reprehended the girl for stea lug the drawers from Mr. Doict's shop, Her mother came down to the police station, and witness then asked the girl in the presence of her mu' her whether she could account for the three aprons produced. The girl then said : " I think my motber made them.' Witness then asked Mrs. Dillon where she had got them from. She replied : "I have made them myself for the baby." Witness then said : " It seems .queer to put the price on them if you make them yourself.' She replied : "There is no mark on them." He then showed her the mark. but she adhered to the statement that she bad made them herself. On Saturday, the 13th October, witness took the aprons to Mrs. Tacker, who kept a stall in the Runcorn Market Hall. She at once identified the articles as being stolen from the stall on Saturday, the 6th October.—The prisoners were re- mandrel until Saturday. being admitted to bail. A Woman WITH • RFOORD,—Ann Corcoran, a character well known by reason of her frequent appearances at toe Police Court, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Brunswick-srreet on the 14th October. —P.O. Wilding gave evidence in support of the charge. The prisoner broke three squares of glass In the window of her sister's house—Sergeant Gregory corroborated. The prisoner, he said, had only come out of gaol the previous Moadey. and she had been drunk every day since.—The Bench fined the prisoner us ar. in , default 14 days' hard labour.
