rington were easily the best up to the finish when the score read. Warrington 2 goals, 4 tries (16 points)! Wigan, lgoal (2 points). Runcorn Defeated at Widnes.

There was great jubilation in the chemical town on Saturday, and notwithstanding the electioneering ex- citement there was corresponding depression over the water, for the pride of Cheshire had come an awful cropper. Widnes, the unlucky, bad risen superior to their overclouded environments, and had vanquished Runcorn by ten points to none. There was an un- doubtedly good cause for rejoicing in the fact, for at the outlock the Widnes prospects were distinctly foreboding. The club's injured list was appalling to contemplate. With the exception of Batey and Rispan every man in the regular back division was unable to play, and Don- nelly was also missing from the forwards. On the other hand Runcorn came with their strongest team, flushed by their victory over Oldham and other distinguished successes ; but on this occasion their lucky star was not in the ascendant. There was half a gale blowing almost from goal to goal, and the Widnes skipper winning the toss naturally took advan- tage, leaving Runcorn to open operations against the full force of the blast. Widnes quickly commenced a vigorous attack, and in some back play Batey made two unsuccessful efforts at goal. The second attempt hit the upright, and on the ball re- bounding Tilley, who followed it with great dash, was near scoring, the sphere being kicked from under him just as he was in the act of grounding it. The game proceeded in ding-long EMT le, Widnes keeping up a continuous attack, which was gallantly met by the de- fenders. At length, from a mark, Batey landed a fine goal,which greatly inspired the Widnesians, and the game had not been long in progrrsa ere Batey placed another goal from a mark. Then Tilley scored in dash- ing style, and Bates., failing to augment, made amends by running ta the line in fine style, and passing at the right moment to MiDanald the latter scored at the corner. No goal resulted. Widnes pressed ta the in- terval, but there was no further scare, and the teams changed ends with Widnes leading by ten points to nothing. Just on the interval Houghton, whose arm had been injured, retired to consult a doctor, and did not return until three-quarter time. This rather spoiled Runcorn's chances of making up the grould they had lost, and, though they played up pluckily and did a good deal of pressing, the defence was too strong for them. Jones put in some very effective runs, and Richardson, Faulkner and Butterworh no several occasions ran and passed very effectively, but the tackling of the home backs was sure, and every attack was safely negotiated. About five minutes from "time," Farmerlwas sent off for using language more f ircible than polite to the referee (VT Ashton of Oldham), but otherwise the game was very pleasantly contested, and the score was a good indication of the merits of the teams :—Widnes, 2 goals 2 tries (10 points) ; Runcorn nothing. Swinton v. Salford.

4' Fully 12,000 people witnessed a very keen tussle be- tween these powerful teams at Swinton. The home side won by four tries—obtained by Hamp.on (two), Morley, and Davies--to two goals (one penalty) and a try. Buckley scored the losers' goals, and T Williams their try.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION. LANCASHIRE SENIOR COMPETITION.
div.p: NORTHERN UNION. LANCASHIRE SENIOR COMPETITION.
Warrington Win at Wigan

The Warrington club distinguished itself Saturday by scoring 16 points to 2 against Wigan on the latter's own ground—a result which was not expected by either side. Wigan were suoposed to have been playing a much improved game of late, but on Saturday they shaped very poorly indeed against the attacks of the Warringtonians. A. strong wind blew across the ground and interfered anry much with the play, kicking especially being a dangerous expedien',. The heavy rain of the morning had cleared off by 3 30, and the afternoon remained fine, the ground also h-ine, in fair condition. Warrington took a strong team with them, and tfn homesters were also fully represented. Mr JEI Smith (Me:bass) was the referee, and the teams lined out as follows. Warrington : Hallam, full back ; Fish, Isherwood. Lawless and Hockenhall, threequarters ; Bate and Bur- gess, half backs ; Taylor, Morrison, Mereweather,Board- man, Eden, Scholtzs, Swift, and Andrews, fowards. Wigan : Anderton, full back ; Nicolson, Eckerslev, , White, and Ball, threequarters ; Owen and Mid ileton, half backs ; Collier, Prescott, W Yates, E Yates, flalli- well, Brown, Hilton, and Peet, forwards. Bate was successful in naming the right side of the coin and Warrington took whatever advantage there was from the choice of positions. Brown started against the wind and kicked into touch at the quarter flag. Taylor punted out and play settled at centre, where the homersters got possession. Lawless lost ground and Warrington were forced to the line, Bur- gess clearing with a punt to Anderten who failed to respond. Isherwood and Eckersley made strong runs for their respective sides, the Wigan man gaining most advantage. Warrington had a let of de- fensive work to do, and did it well, while they occasion- ally worked down to the other end. Wigan had some advantage forward for a time, and by keeping the ball close they bottled Warrington up. Fish was entirely neglected and eventually crossed the field and made play for himself. He was uncommonly active, and be- fore long he caused an invasion of the home hale. Isherwood found himself on the wing, and Fish passing smartly, Isherwood scored at the corner. Fish took the goal-kick but failed. The success did Warrington good and they were soon seeking more points. The forwards played with great dash and An- derton again mulling his catch afereweather registered a try under the posts, Fish landing a goal. Wigan made a brief visit to the other end, and Anderton had a fruitless shot at goal from Yates' mark.Mereweather got away at centre and passed to Morrison ,who knocked on. Play was in midfield when Isherwood smartly threw to Fish, who outpaced all opposition, dodged Anderton on the line, and scored a brilliant try. Isherwood kicked a goal, and at half time Warrington led by 2 goals 3 tries (13 points) to Wigan nil. Taylor re-started and the home team again got the upper hand by determined play. Fish did some excel- lent work on the left, and it was owing to his efforts that Wigan made so little headway. Lawless and Hockenhall passed well ht times, and the wing man had bard luck to lose possession on the line. NICOISOII got away and kicked when challenged, Hilton taking the ball off-side and running between the Warrington posts. He was penalised for his temerit , and Warrington cleared. Wigan rushed down again, and only Hallam's pluck saved a try. The attack was maintained, and at last Anderton landed a goal from a penalty. This was Wigan's only point, for Warring- ton soon sent them to the right-about. Fish made another grand attempt to score, but numbers prevailed, and he was grassed at the corner. Nicolson nut in another good sprint for the Wiganers, Isherwood knock- ing him in touch at the quarter flag. Warrington attacked again, and Bite bluffing his opponents scored the fourth try. Fish missed an easy shot at goal. War-

div.head: LANCASHIRE "A" TEAMS COMPETITION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE "A" TEAMS COMPETITION.
Warrington Easily Defeat Wigan.

The " A" team from the colliery town visited Wilderspool enclosure on Saturday afternoon and returned home vanquished to the extent of 37 points to nil. About 1,500 specteors witnessed the match, which did not commence until a quarter of an hour after the advertised time, owing to the late arrival of the visitors. Wigan started with ten men, the remainder arriving later in the afternoon. The spin of the coin was in favour of Warrington, who played with the wind to their backs during the first half. Immeliately after the kick-off, Wigan made a rush into the home team's quarters, but were repulsed, and play was soon carried to the vicinity of the visitors' goal. From a scrimmage, Ratcliffe got pos- session and scored Warrington's first try, the kick at goal being a failure. On resuming Warrington main- tained their attack and after a splendid run down the field, Knight ccored near the corner. No goal resulted. Ratcliffe again distinguished himself and scored a fine'try between the posts, the goal kick being successful. The Wiganers now invaded the Warrington territory but were speedily driven back. A. scrimmage took place near the Wigan line, and Jewkes got over. Garrity made an abortive attempt at goal. Warrington con- tinucd to have matters all their own vay, and Ratcliffe came within an ace of scoring but was grassed. div.head: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.
div.p: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.
Runcorn Wesleyans v. Flint Shop Assistants.

These association teams met on the Canal-street ground on Wednesday afternoon, and enjoyed a spirited and exhilarating game, at the conclusion of which Flint were declared the winners by 2 goals to 1 goal. Earlestown Rovers v: Prescot Juniors.

Played at Prescot on Saturday. The Juniors bad the benefit of a strong wind during the first half but at the interval the Rovers were leading by one to nothing. On resuming the Rovers scored again and then the home- stets had a turn, their forwards piling on three goals in about a quarter of an hour. Just before the finish Broster put the teams on an equality from a penalty kick. Broster scored all the Rovers goals and the home centre forward scored all the Prescot goals.
Bangor v. Newton-le-Willows. COMBINATION.

At Bangor, before a poor gate. At the outset tbe visitors made headway, and for a brief period were operating in close quarters. Toe defence fought hard to keep their charge_ intact. Billy Lewis got the home team on the move, but Dauiton returned, and from a long range Kenny scored. Hot pressure was brought to bear on Horrocks, and after repeated attempts Jimmy Jones eventually put the elevens on equal terms. Hop- kins again brought play to dangerous quarters.Horrocks saved a thunderbolt from J Roberts. The same minute Dick Jones, after a clever run, topped the bar with a terrific shot. Kenny and Buller traveilea beautifully to a certain point when Edwards' Neneralship came out on top. The game was most spirited, and on both sides the attack was of the highest order. Kenny give Lee a splendid opening, but he arrived too late. VVorrall, however, was more successful, and his final effort de- served batter hick. For several minutes the home for- wards showered shots on florrocks, but be coped well with the determined efforts of the front rank. Dick Jones eventually found the net, but he was ruled off- side. Buckland put the Willows ahead. Half-time— Newton 2, Bangor 1. The game ended in a draw of 2 goals each. Earlestown v. St. Helens Recs.

This friendly encounter was played on the Mesnes ground on Satnrday. The question is often asked which is the best league as regards foatball displays— cambination or Lancashire League? This match provided an answer in a mild sort of way. Mild, because friendlies are very rarely anything to go by, and this was no exc.ption to the rule. The Recs were without Joe Lee their custodian, and Ellaby, one of their half- backs. Earlestown were fully represented, a new man named Saunders being tried at right inside. Earlestown won the toss and curiously enough Chew deeided to give the Rees the benefit of the wind and hill for the first half. The homesters were however, the first t 3 become dangerous, Leach cleverly eluding Hodton and giving Rowley a warm handful which the custodian negotiated in masterly style. The Recs forwards next had a turn at attacking, but Chew and 'his backs pre- , sented a stubborn defence and easily kept them at bay. ' However, after 15 minutes play. the Rees' right wing got away, and after Muir had beaten the backs, Chew ran out to meet him, but the ReC3 man got the ball first andripped it neatly round the custodian into the net The homesters livened up a little after this, but could make no impression on the Recs. defence, and the inter- val arrived with the visitors leading by the odd goal. The sacond half saw the Recs. acting on the defensive for /practically the whole of the moiety, but from a couple of breakaways Kelly and Davies put on points for them. On the other hand Earlestown could only score once, this being the result of a' well placed corner by Settle, the ball bitting Linton full in the face and rebounding into the net. The whistle therefore blew with the Recs. winners of a moderate game by three goals to one. The game on the whole was slightly above the average friendly, but very little excitement was evinced by the spectators. The homesters were a great deal better on the day's play than the Rees, although the score was against them. The new man. Saunders. played a very fair game, but will improve when he gets used to his partners.

div.head: DEATH OF Mr. CLAUDE J. MORRIS, J.P.
div.p: DEATH OF Mr. CLAUDE J. MORRIS, J.P.
Funeral on Friday.

The remains of the deceased gentleman were on Friday conveyed by rail from Buxton to Man- chester and afterwards by road to the Manchester Crematorium, Didsbury, where they were cremated in the presence of a large number of mourners who had known and respected the late Mr Morris during his lifetime. The cortege was met at the gates of the Crematorium by the Rev Dr Mackennal of Bowdon, who conducted the service at 3-15, and referred in eulogistic terms to the deceased. He was, said the rev gentleman, a friend not only to those he employed but to everyone else with whom he came in contact.

The chief mourners were Mr L Gordon Rvlands, Mr W Peter Rylands, Mr J Paul Rylands, Mr Edward Rylands, Mr G N Ford, Mr Lewis Marriott, Mr C A Tatham, the Rev R Row, of Buxton, and the Rev W M Arthur. Toe foll Owing were also present :—Messtos W B Butler, Wilfred Williams (Birmingham), A G Symonds, S A Fulda,E Johnson (Manchester), A Murray, A Doughty, Junr. (Liver- pool), Lewis W Reynolds (Thelwall), Charles Henderson (Glasgow), W Carson (Warrington), F Jevons (Liverpool), G Mason, T D Hall, J Fergus (Glasgow). W Armitage, A Allan Paton, F W Killick, A E Patterson, J J Bleckly, W M Arthur, R H Watts, J R Paton (Liverpool), F Smith (Halifax), E C Foster, and C Brockbank. The firm were represented by Messrs. Nield, Whittaker, Farrar, Wadsworth, Maddock and Webb (managers) Jeffary (late manager), Mc.Quire (trav- eller)! Dakin, Knott, Happle, Plevin, Gibson, Whit. ham, Sutton, and Beckett.

A larg,e number of wreaths were sent by rela- tives and friends of the deceased and among them were one from the staff of Messrs Rylands Bros, Limited, one from the employees of the firm, and another from the Iran and Steel Wire Association.

div.head: APPROACHING MUNICIPAL
div.p: THE APPROACHING MUNICIPAL
ELECTIONS.

Now that the Parliamentary election is over interest is being aroused in the approaching muni- cipal elections. At the present moment, Latchford ward is without its full number of representatives in the Town Council owing to the death of Coun- cillor Lee. He was one of the councillors who would have retired at the forthcoming municipal election and on his death it was decided to leave the vacancy open until November No steps have yet been taken by the Conservatives to adopt a candidate, but a meeting of the ward committee will be called as soon as notice of the vacancy has been given. By the agreement which was come to by the two political parties it is understood that no opposition will be offered to any of the nominees of the two par Lies. This, of course, will not prevent independent can- didates entering the field, and it will be remem- bered that several were brought forward by the Ratepayers and Property Owners Associa- tion last November. The Councillors who retire this year are as follows : Town Hall Ward: James Smethurst (C) Whitecross Ward: George Plumpton (TA) Bewsey Ward : William Pierpoint (L) Orford Ward : Arthur Peaco7,k (L) St. John's Ward: Frederic R Roberts (IA) Fairfield Ward: Alfred Woods (C) Howley Ward: John Evans (C) St. Austin's Ward; John Crosfield (L) Latchford Ward : We understand that in two or three of the wards the retiring members frill not seek re-election. It is, however, too early to make any definite an- nouncement of their names.

div.head: UHINA.
div.p: UHINA.
Manchuria Annexed by
Russia.

The " Daily Telegraph "St. Petersburg cor- respondent telegraphed on Wednesday:—Russia has annexed Manchuria, whatever official denials may have beeu issued. No dementis can dispose of the fact. The correspondent cites many facts in sup- port of this definite statement, and quotes a member of the Russian Military Council that for two years not a single soldier or warship will be recalled from the Far East, where there are 300,000 Muscovites now under arms.

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS.
More Fighting. J. De Wet Killed.

The" Standard" correspondent at Pretoria telegraphs on Tuesday :—Botha and Steyn, en- deavouring to break through from the bush veldt, were met by General Lyttelton south- west of Lydenburg. After a short engagement the Boers retired towards Pietersburg. The Boer Commandant was wounded. Lyttelton. is retiring to Lydenburg. Forty men of the West Kent Regiment sur- rounded a small laager near Grant Platz. Seven Boers were killed, including J. De Wet, and eighteen taken prisoners. We had one wounded.

div.head: Mr Kruger. To Sail on Saturday.
div.p: Mr Kruger. To Sail on Saturday.

A "Daily Mail" telegram dated L3urenco Marques, Wednesday says:—The Dutch cruiser Gelderland will finish coaling to-morrow, and will sail on Saturday with Mr Kruger. The " Daily Mail " Marseilles correspondent telegraphed :—Dr Leyds has arranged that Kruger will disembark here, and the captain of the Gelderland has.been instructed accordingly. Kruger will afterwards visit Toulon and Paris, and the Boer agency is organising sym-;)athetic demonstrations. Leyds and the Boer delegates are still sanguine of continental intervention.

div.head: St. Helens Football President at
div.p: The St. Helens Football President at
the Front. Letter to the Team.

Mr. J. H. Houghton,secretary of the St. Helens Rugby Club, on Saturday, received a letter from Captain Michael Hughes, of Sherdley Hall, the president of the club, who has been in South Africa on Lord Roberts's staff, since the beginning of the year. The letter was read to the members of the team on Saturday,previous to the game with Oldham. Gswain Hughes, writing from Krugersdorp, on September 18th, returned thanks for his re-election as president of the club, and congra- tulates the committee and players on the phenomenally successful season the club brought to a close shortly after his departure from England. He was only sorry that he bad been able to do so very little for the benefit or encouragement of the club, but it did not happen every winter that one was called upon to leave home and proceed 7,000 miles to form a target for a farmer who is also a marksman. He trusted in the future to make up for his absence during the past season if he was not destined to leave his bones on the veldt. He met one of the members of the team (Carney) serving in the Militia when Mrs. Hughes and be passed through Norval's Pont in May. He had not heard whether that particular regiment bad been allowed to go further up- country or not. Mrs. Hughes was working very hard in No. 9 hospital at Bloemfontein, and she had not missed a day except an occasional Sunday since she entered Broemfontein early in May, and bad attended both enteric cases and wounded soldiers. Mrs. Hughes had lately been giving evidence before the Commission appointed to inquire into the hospital management question. Captain Hughes says he has served in the field under the different ;.,,enerals.and hrd not only been in Pretoria and Johannesburg. but had also been with General French, and was the first to ride back to Pre- toria with despatches f,sr Lord Roberts, doing the hun- dred miles in two days.

div.head: Treatment of our Soldiers at
div.p: The Treatment of our Soldiers at
the Front.
A,'WarrinGton Man's Opinion of Grumblers.

Dear Mr. Editor, myself and many of my comrades would be extremely obliged if you could find space to publish my letter in your valuable paper. Many of our heroes who have been invalided home from the front, are idling their time away siftinz all kinds of frivolous complaints from their war-worn brains. Poor fellows ! I cannot help but think that they have been hard done to, for one gallant hero, be- longing to my regiment, had such a large amount of hardships stored away in his haversack, that on his arrival in England, he staggered with his burden to a reporter, who gladly relieved him of his load. The re- porter put his sorrows on paper, and strange to say, the paper held them, for some of the words were RO heavy, that it was wonderful that they did not sink through the paper ; some of my readers may have relatives at present in South Africa, but they may ease their minds, as to our treatment during the war. I belong to the Ist South Lancashire Regiment, lam still serving with my regiment. I have been well clothed throughout the campaign. The food I have had has been all that any ordinary man could wish for. lam enjoying good health. I have experienced a few rough times and sleepless ;nights, but I have always met these things with the courage of an Irishman, for such I am. To make a long story short, I have nothing to grumble about. A few days ago we had just completed a rather long march, between Wakkerstroom and Utrecht. I was preparing a nice dish of Quaker Oats, whilst my comrade was arranging our bed for the night, He had received a letter that day,also a slip of newspaper which he asked me to read. This is what I gathered from the paper : that the writer belonged to my regiment, that he is known by the name of "Tim." That he is in Eng- land and has been for some months. That he found that the hospitals were not quite the way he liked ; that the food was beastly, the biscuits being very hard ; that the water he drank was out of the river ; that he had been under shot and shell whilst the lightning flashed and the thunder roared. But through want of time or something else he forgot to tell the people, that he had not been in a single engagement, and he had not enough brains to tell himself, that some of his comrades would shake new life into him, were he here. Now, dear raaders, you should ignore all those hungry and bootless letters, and you may rest assured that all your friends in South Africa, are looked after far better than in any previous campaign. As dinner is now ready, and as the saying goes "he who hesitates is lost " I must draw my letter to a close, thanking the Editor for his kindness in publishing my letter.—l remain yours truly. A WARRINGTONIAN, Private Truth, Ist South Lancashire Regiment.
General Baden-Powell's Advice to Runcorn Boys. Interesting Letter.

The subjoined letter from Major Gmeral Baden • Powell appeared in the "Runcorn Parish Magazine" for October. It should be explained that a "League of Health and Manliness " has been formed in the parish of Weston the members of which promise not to smoke before they are 21 at least. The Rev WTI Stables is the president. The letter appended is in reply to a request from fifteen members of the League—most of them choir boys,past and present —who wrote to the distinguished soldier asking him to become their patron. Rustenbum Transvaal, 23rd July. 1900.

My dear Boys,—l was very glad indeed to get your kind congratulations on the relief of Mafeking. I am very glad to be elected patron of your club—snd I have three reasons for taking special interest in it. Firstly, because I was myself for five years Is choir boy in the Charterhouse choir. Secondly. because I am not a smoker. Thirdly, because I was partly educated as a boy at Northwich, and used often to go over to Runcorn. So you see I feel qualified to take a more than outside interest in your doings. I quite agree with your prin- ciples, that it is at your time of life that your habits and rharacter are formed and remain yours during your manhood. A feeble youth who smokes because he thinks

And I think that if boys would take • the line cf always trying to do.what is their duty it would become, in a short time, part of their nature, and would thus guide every action of theirs as men. You who are choir boys, or past choir boys, will recog- nise that if each sings his part in tin harmony under the direction of the leader—that is, if each one does his duty—the result is a pleasing anthem, whereas if each sang what he liked best there would be a fine old cat's chorus. So it is in life—if each does his duty in his proper line or profession the whole community moves pro iperously and suecessfully. Fellows are very often in doubt as to which of two curses may be the proper one to take, or are tecipted to take one line because it is more pleasant or my thin the one which their conscience tells them is the right one. Well, if ever you are in such doubt there is an east way of de- ciding, and that is to ask your conscience •‘ Which is it my duty to do ? ' and that will nearly always guide you ri4ht. In this way you wilt soon find that it comes as a habit to do your duty to your leader, whether that be the choirmaster, the head of your department, em- ployer, or efficer, or the Queen. And remember always that in thus doing, conscientiously, your duty to your leader, you are also doing your duty to God. And also remember that as you lads may often—without know- ing it perhaps—be imitating the examples of men before you, so also unknown to you there may be, and pro- bably are, other boys watching you and imitating your example. So let your example to them be always a good one. In this way the whole of England's boys and men will in a short time be what the best of them now are, viz., a lot living honourably up to what their con- science telis them is their duty.—Wishing the club every success. Mariners' Church, Runcorn.

The harvest festival of this place of worship com- menced on Friday ev‘?ning, with a special sermon preached by the Rev N J Poole, BA . curate of Holy Trinity, Runcorn. In the aaternoon of Sunday the Rev. E 8 Oliver, A..,preached a thoughtful sermon from the text" Whatsoever a man sows that shall he alma reap." The children belonging to the Sunday school sang a num- ber of special harvest hymns, and the service was alto- gether of a helpful character. In the evening the pul- pit was occupied by Mr M Hall, of Birkenhead, who founded a practical sermon en the parable of the sower. The church was crowded. As in previous years a festive appearance was added to the interior of the church, by means of beautiful dec)rations. A profusion of flowers, fruit, corn, had been utilized to tha best possible advantage, the communion rails, reading desk, pulpit, and window sills,havinglhad a large amount of time and labour spent upon them. Immediately under the reading desk and pulpit small tables were arranged on which were displayed an abut.idauce of fruit.

The harvest thanksgiving services in connection with the above mission commenced on Thursday. 'rho churcl was prettily decorated with fruit, flowers, and corn. The preacher was the Rev G McNeil, chaplain of the cadet ship Conway, who gave a very instructive address. On Sunday the services were cputinued, the preacher being the Rev W H S:ables. div.head: SERIOUS FARM FIRE.
div.p: SERIOUS FARM FIRE.
Shippons Destroyed at Appleton.

A serious outbreak of fire occured on the premises of Mr John Whitlow, Broomfield's Farm, Appleton, near Stockton Heath, shortly before ten o'clock on Tuesday night. It was discovered joct as Mr Whitlow and the family were about to retire to rest and the VVilderspool and Warrington Fire Brigades were at once communi- cated with. A full complement of men promptly turned out and soon arrived at the scene of the fire. Fortun- ately a good supply of water was obtained and the fire- men lost no time in commencing operations. The fire broke out in a loft over one of the shippons, and a good deal of farm produce was destroyed and a number of implements damaged. Most of the shippons were burnt to the ground. All the cattle, to the number of from 30 to 35, were got out safely and sent into the fields. At one time it was thought that the house itself was in danger, but happily the firemen succeeded in confining the flames to the outbuildings. Both brigades were kept busily engaged until five o'clock on Wednesday morning, and a few firemen re- mained throughout the day. The place presented a most desolate appearance. A gigantic pile of debris was the remains of the principal outbuilding, and, as it con- tinued to smoulder, bad to be carefully watched. About noon it was decided to remove what was possible from it, and the firemen were then able easily to complete their task • It is impossible to give a definite estimate of the amount of the damage but it must amount to several thousand pounds. Fortunately the loss is fully covered by insurance. The origin of the fire is at present a mystery, as all the outbuildings were visited shortly beforn the family retired to rest,and there was then not the sli2hteat indication that such a serious calamity was about to befall them.

Hamilton School Boys' Swimming Club. During the summer an average of over 100 mem- bers of this club have each week visited the firs., class plunge bath at the Corporation Baths, Lee- street, the Baths Committee having issued tickets at reduced prices. Last Friday 130 members were present and a swimming gala took place, the prizes offered consisting of silver medals, pocket knives, pens, &c. For the club championship there were nine entries and an exciting struggle was witnessed in the final. W Fogg came in first, T Berry being second, H Gatley third, and W Price fourth. In the one breadth handicap J Derbyshire obtained the first position J Johnson coming in second and A Grime third. W Brookes gained the first prize for the neatest, dive, T Berry and W Fogg being second and third respectively. A scramble across the bath, for non- swimmers, caused mnch amusement, J Heacock coming in first, 3 Helsom second, and H Lythgoe third. A costume and candle race was another in- tere.ting event and resulted in a win for E Lunt, R Stanistreet being second. II Gatley carried off the silver medal which was offered to the boy show- ing the most improvement during the season. Prof. Barlow capably discharged the duties of judge, and jllr Frank II Longshaw rendered great assistance.

div.head: PRESENTATION AT NEWTON.
div.p: PRESENTATION AT NEWTON.

At the Legh Arms Hotel, Newton. on Friday evening, a gathering of the office staff of Messrs. McCorquodale and Co.,Newtln was held:for the pur- pose of presenting Mr W Gee, with some token of their esteem on his transfer to the firm's London house of business. The presentation took the form of a gentleman's dressing bag, fitted with the necessary requisites. Mr Adams tendered the present to Mr Gee on behalf of the office staff, and wished him every success in his new sphere. The evening was spsnt in a convivial manner, several toasts being honoured, and songs renderei at intervals.

HUSSAR TROOP DINNER ATINEWTON. The annual dinner of "C " trop tiancashire Hussars was held at the Pied Bull Hotel on Satur- day evening. There was a good muster, amongst the civilians present being Mr A C Leslie (agent to Lord Newton), Nir F J Wood, Mr G Clarke, Dr Wat- kins and Rev J Ryder. After the edibles had been disposed of, and the cloth removed, the subsequent proceedings were presided over by Mr Leslie, the vice-chair being occupied by Sergeant Major Pierce. The ,asual loyal toasts were proposed and duly honoured, the "Health of Lord Newton," being pro- posed by Dr Watkins. The evening was very pleasantly spent, songs being given by Messrs T Norris,and T A Ritchie. Trooper Hales pre- sided at the piano. APPRENTICES' DINNER AT EARLESTOWN.

A very pleasant social gathering tooic place at the Viaduct Hotel on Saturday night, on the occa- sion of four apprentices employed in the Fitting Shop at the Viaduct Works completing their period of apprenticeship. About 40 workmen were present, together with the four apprentices, Messrs Roberts, Pearson, Grimshaw and Mottram, and an excellent dinner was partaken of. Mr W Sutton pre-ided at the subsequent proceedings, and in a few opening remarks dwelt upon the occasion of their gathering. A number of toasts were proposed and honoured,in- eluding the "Health of the Apprentices," the hope that they would be steady and attentive to their work being expressed. Several songs were given by several of those present, and a very enjoyable time was spent. PROPERTY SALE AT EARLESTOWN.

At the Wellington Hotel on Tuesday evening, before a good company, several lots of valuable pro- perty were sold by auction. Lot 1 consisted of a semi-detached villa situate at 69, Cross-lane, Earles- town, in the occupation of the owner. The tenure is leasehold for a term of 999 years from March 231 h, 1866, at the low yearly ground rent of £1 10s. The bidding started at .£3OO, and WAS carried on to £355, at which price it was knocked down to Mr T Lytfigoe.—The second lot was the corner shop and dwelling-house, No. 42, Brookfield-street, Earles- town, occupied by MiQs M A Halson. Starting at £l5O it slowly rose to £l9O, at which price it was withdrawn. The other lot was the dwelling-house 93, Market-street, Earlestown, occupied by Mr J Andrews, the estimated rental being £25 per year. The bidding commenced at £3OO, and at £365 it was withdrawn.

div.head: GOOD TEMPLARY.
div.p: GOOD TEMPLARY.

The Hope of Earlestown Lodge meeting was held in Wargrava Hall on Monday evening. Bro Clarke, ES, presiding in the absence of Bro Cutler, CT, who was ill. One candidate was received as an ancient templar. Report of the Anniversary Com- mittee was read and adopted, and Bros Woods, Sharp,Roberts, Newman and Warburton and Sisters Owen, Grant, Woods, Ord, Thomas, and Hall appoin- ted to sell tickets.—Bro Newman gave the report of the No. 1 Convention held at Wigan, which was adopted. Bro Newman also gave the greetings which he had received from the following Lodges in India :—Seychell Lodge. No. 64; Kings Own, No. 58; Herald of Hope, No. 36; Goodwill Lodge. No. 7; Randrv. Ceylon; Little Pioneers Juvenile Temple, No. 425; Kandy, India. The greetings were ordered to be entered on the minutes; Bro Newman to answer them. All joined in singing Ode 230; reading Bro Newman ; piano solo, Bro Willis ; address, Bro J Leatherbarrow ; song, "Good-bye at the door," Sister Owens; reading, Bro G Clarke ; recitation by a brother from Onward Lodge, War- rington ; song. "She wore a wreath of roses," Sister Morley; reading Bro Roberts. The lodge was closed in the usual manner by Bro Clarke.

div.head: CATROLIC BAZAAR.
div.p: CATROLIC BAZAAR.

The congregation and friends of the Sacred Heart Roman Catholic Church, St. Helens, are this week engaged in a great effort to secure a large reduction in the debt of 0,000 which rests on their elementary and Sunday schools. Headed by Father Hearne, rector, the congregation have arranged a grand bazaar, which opeeed at the Town Hall on Tuesday. The various stalls represent the various colonies, the title being the " Empire Bazaar." The Mayor, Couueillor Beecham, performed the opening ceremony, and similar services were rendered on Wednesday by Sir David Gamble, Bart., CB; en Thursday by Mr Se`on-Karr, M.P. Moe- ,' signor Carr, Vicar-General, presided over a large atten- dance at the opening ceremony. Amongst those p,.esent ' were Councillors Henry Martin, J Berchall, H B Bates. W Molyneux. J Green, J Co!lins, T M'Lachlan, and J Fisher, the Rev Father Hearne (rector of Sacred Heart) the Rev Father Widdowson (rector of Lowe House). the Rev Father Crank (Chorley), &e. Monsignor Carr bricfly asked the Mayor be open the bazaar.—His Wor- ship, who was received with applause, said it was not necessary to be a co-religionist of theirs to sympathise with and aid their noble efforts in the cause of popular education, and anyone who was in a position like his must especially rejoice at the splendid results which had been attained and achieved by the Rector of the Sacred Heart in the erection of the Father Dobso^ Schools, which had been erected to the memory of Father Dahlson, their late worthy and deeply-regretted rector. The work had been carried on at a vast expenditure, and the money ought to be found. If they had a sehool board in the town instead of voluntary scheolsAthe ratepayers would have to pay annually a greater aam than was necessary to naP lc, that baz tar a success. He was told that it was the first occasion that Sacred Heart had appealed to the public, and he felt sure that the first appeal would not be in vain, end that the townspeople would not fail to respond to it.—The Rev Father Hearne proposed a vet, of thanks to Mr Beecham, and Mr George Scott scconded. The resolution was passed unanimously.—Tho Rev Father Crank proposed, and the Rev Father Widdowson seconded, a vote of thanks to Monsignor Carr for nresiding.—The bazaar will also be continued to-day (Friday) and to-morrow.

div.head: RUNCORN TECHNICAL INSTITUTE.
div.p: THE RUNCORN TECHNICAL INSTITUTE.

Distribution of Prizes by the Lord Bishop of Chester. Mr. William Handley, J.P., chairman of the Runcorn Urban District Council, presided on Wedeesday night over a well attended gathering of parents and general public, assembled in the new wing of the Runcorn Technical Institute, the occasion being the annual dis- tribution of prizes to the successful scholars attending the evening classes. He was supported by the Right Rev Dr Jayne, Bishop of Chester, Rev Canon Wool, Messt, J Wilson, F Wiswall, F A Lake, E Marshall, G Hewitt, E Irnison, J Pritchard, F W Hutton, T A Lawrenson (headmaster), and J Mr. E. Marshall, at the outset, announced that a com- munication from the E lucational Department had been received intimating that the certificates won by the students could not be forwarded that week, so that they would not be presented by His Lordship that night. It was the first time the Departm eat had disappointed them. Mr. W. Handley who was cordially received, said be- fore calling upon the Lord Bishop of Chester, whom they all gladly welcomed as a friend and well-wisher in their work of T, chnical Instruction, he had thought it might be of some little interest to refer to the work of the schools ia its local aspect and its probable influence as a teaching centrecthe more se as they had not had the advantage of perusing the admirable and concise report prepared by their secretary. (Hear, hear:) Of the day schools which were established some three years ago, it was scarcely necessary to speak,as a few weeks ago they had its own special prize day on which occasion an address was delivered and the prizes distributed by Mr. Roger Bate, the vice-chairman of the Technical Instruc- tion Committee of the Cheshire County Council. Since that day they hal reeeived the annual grant awarded the day schools by the Board of Education and Science and Art Department amounting to £299 5s 61 as compared with £231. 16s 7d in the previous year. That represented a sum of £4 19s. for each student examined, and he thought he was cor- rect in stating that that was the highest grant earned since the establishment of the day scnool, and refl,cted great credit on the teaching staff, and the industry of the Day School studsnts. That was supp:emented by a grant from the County Council of £lo3—a County Coun- cil second to none in its support, and encouragement of E lucation. (Hear, hear.) That night they were met more immediately in the interests of the evening classes, which was taught in that building. Classes had now been taught in the Institute for the past five years though good work was dene for several years previously under somewhat difficult and hampering conditions as regards suitability of premises and adequate teaching appliances, but it was this work which laid the founda- tion of the Technical Instruction of to day.— Technical Instruction in suitable premises and with adequate appliances, might be said to date from the birth of the Institute. An old proverb ran "A -new broom sweeps clean," and the opening of the now Institution in its first year naturally attracted a large number of students. It had been true of their institute. 'raking the number of students in the aggregate. In the first session 1895-5, the number on the register was 508. of whom 177 presented themselves for examination. In the last session 1899-1900, the number on the register was 478, of whom 171 were examined. In 1895-6 the largest classes, with 249 on the register, were in what are called Tec ecological classes, containing principally students in cookery and dressmaking ; and the smaller classes were in the more numerously sub-divided Science and Art Sections, with 259 on the register. In the last session the increasing number of students in the Science and Art Sections had almost entirely made up for the smaller number attending the Techao- logical Classes. The register contained the nany.4l of 357 in the Science and Art Sectioas, and of 131 in the Technological. These figurea surely pointed to the increasing usefulness of the Institute. As the growth was in what might be termed without offence, the snore serious subjects, those formed with the express object of helping our young men and maidens t) win their way in the battle of life. lie might also mention that eight Building Construction S:udents had taken honours. (Cheers.) The grants received during the year from the Board of Educatioa and the Science and Art Department exceeded those of the previous year by £34; amounting to £ll6 8s 61 which may be taken as a certificate of the ability of both teachers and taught. The:County Council assisted their evening work by a generous grant of £347 12s 9d, to whom their gratefu thanks were due, asiwithout that aid it would be im- possible for them to carry on the work of the Technical Instrucion Classes. Referring to the financial s'de of the work Mr. Handley said : From the statement of accounts which included the receipts and expenditure both of the Day and Evening Schools, as made up from April Ist 1839, to March 31st, 1900, he found that ex— cluding treasurer's balances and what may be called ex- traordinary receipts they received for the last year:- 2 s. d. Grants from the County Council 450 12 9 Grants from the Board of Education and S.A. Department Fees from Day and Evening Students Miscellaneous receipts 5 12 5 From the Proceeds of the Id rate allowed to them .. l9l 7 0

On the expeaditura sido, ex3luding extraordinary pay- ments, they had paid for Salaries of Teachers and Officers 1039 0 2 Apparatus and Books Printing, Stationery, Cleaning, Lighting and Repairs Chemicals and Sundries, Miscellaneous Expenses
A total of 1450 8 10

leaving a small credit balance for depreciation and replacement. That truly might be called a satisfactory expenditure of the pubic He thought Ps was Shakespeare who had said "He who opens a school closes a prison." Ho felt they had been trying to dispel the darkeess and let in light by their labours. He would not longer inter- vene between these present and the Lord Bishop of Chester. for on all matters educational he was an acknowledged authority and they would all listen to his words of wisdom with pleasure and profit. (Applause.) The Bish®p said it was a very real pleasure and privi- lege to anyone who was interested in education or interested in the social and moral welfare of a town like Runcorn to come and sea such a sight as he saw that evening—all those bright young faces gathered together with the sympathy and support and approval of the seniors and senators of the town and in the midst of this excelleec building and appliances. As far as he was able to judge and to think the young ones were starting their life with opportunities that their elders had never dreamed of when they were young. He said that in all sincerity many of them were educated at a very good school. He was educated at an admirable school himself, but the sort of appliances they had now-a-deys in institutions like this, were never dreamed of. It was a very delightful thing to come and see them starting life in the midst of all these advan- tages. and he would congratulate the town of Runcorn upon having risen to their opportunities and responsi- bilitie +—he •nrant the leading spirits—and provided such an equipment as this. He sometimes thought,ancl he believed other people sometimes thought, that a town the size of Runcorn was at a considerable disadvantage as compared with towns of larger population. In this respect that they had not so many rich people to make bountiful gifts to the-n; very many of their wealthy people lived at a distance ; and then the population was:not large enough to enable them to raise very large sums from the rates, and of course rates were not always the most popular things with ratepayers. But in spite of these difficulties they in Runcorn appeared to have risen to the situation and to have berne the pressure of rates willingly and gladly and to have done the very best they could and a very conspicuous and valuable hest it seemed to him. If he were not mistaken it was not the only institution in Runcorn which did so much for the education of the people of Runcorn, There was the free libr try not only fcr youths but for grown up people as well. He knew what excellent institutions these were : Institutions of this sort were instances of most justifiable socialism. As Lord Salisbury has said on this point, they were all sucialists now-a-days and who did not agree with socialism to the extent it was shown in the Technical Inctitetion and the Free Library ? What were the reasons why the youth of the nation—the trustees of property as Lord Beaconsfield described them —should make use of the ad- vantages that were brought before them, whether they belonged to the day school or fre- quented the night school? There were three reasons why those present and others who were not present should use these advantages as largely as they could. The first motive which would tell with them was the motive of patriotism. If our country was to maintain and keep pre-eminence amongst the nations of the world we must be educating ourselves in order to keep at least on a level with them, not out of mere rivalry and competition but because it was unbecoming an Englislamen to be behindhand in the race of know- ledge and of mental and manual training of Art and Scierce in all departments. If were true English- men and Englishwomen we must feel it to be a patriotic duty to equip ourselves so as worthily to represent that great nation, to which by the Providence of God they belonged. Then there was what he might call—it was a good honest working name—the bread and butter motive, a most justifiable motive and one which they all recognised. They had to make their way in life ; they bad to earn their tread ; they had to win their place in order that in the place they did win they might do good service, not re.erely to them- selves but to others—to the country and to God who had placed them in that station. The bread and butter motive ought to stir them up to do their bast to use these appliances and advantages which were now breught within their reach. If they did not use them now they would not be quite able to make up for opper- Waits' lost, and it was the duty of every man to keep the bread and butter motive prominently before his mind. They were justified in winning their position in

life if they won it henourably and worthily. Then there was the motive of the love of knowledge. Though many of those who attended the different classes were think- ing mainly of qualifying themselves for seme examios- tion, or some branch ot work in which they were engaPe l, and the chance of a higher appointment must be prominent and almost predominant in their minds, yet surely as they progressed in the different branches of study, they learned to love knowledge for itself—they gained an enthusiasm for know- ledge. He did not want to see them looking to their studies merely and exclusively from the " getting on in the world" point of view, though that in its proper place was a justifiable motive enough. They should endeavour to lift the level of life and know- ledLie by degrees. They had not the whole population ofittuneorn studying at that admirable institution. In- deed, it was only a comparatively small proportion. For instance thqro were some 103 individua students in the day schcol ; 63 in the school of art ; 131 in techno- logy. Well what did it mean ? It meant the lifting of the level of knowledge all round ; and what a great thing they accomplished when they lifted the level of things in any department. His Lordship in conclu ling spoke of the way knowledge was diffused and elevated by the efforts of the few serious students who went forth into other spheres. They were wise enough to know that "a little knowledge was a dangerous tv.if4,," but a little knowledge if used as a steeping stone to other and more complete knowledge ; in that sense a little knowledge was anything but dangf r- oue. Their study ,ught to constantly improve their powers of appreciation and value ofjthings and oug.nt to cause them to live up to a higher moral and mental tone. (Applause) His Lordship having presented the prizes to the successful students whose names we published a short time ago, Mr J Wilson proposed that tho best thanks of the meeting and the best thanks of the Technical Committee be accorded his Lordship for distributing the prizes and for his address.
Mr F W Hutton seconded, and the vote was accorded with acclamation. A vote of thanks to the Chairman con cu led the proceedings.

div.head: ROYAL WELSH LADIES' CHOIR AT PARR HALL.
div.p: THE ROYAL WELSH LADIES' CHOIR AT PARR HALL.

Despite the unfavourable weather of Monday evening there was a large audience in the Parr Hall to hear the Royal Welsh Ladies' Choir on th -ir return visit to War- rington. The frost seats were rather scantily filled but the other parts of the hall were well patronised and the financial result must have been considered very satisfac- tory unddr the circumstances. The commencement of the concert was delayed for a short time in consequence of an irritating noise in the heating apparatus. There was a rapidly recurring " clink-clank " and other noises peculiar to hot-water pipes. The choir was ready to give the first item on the programme but under such conditions it was impossibie t iproceeã and it was some twenty minutes after the advertised time for the con- cert to commence ere the noisy interrupter could be quietened. The choir 26 in number, occupied an im- provised gallery on the platform and opened the pro- gramme by a capi'al renderiag of " Rule Britannia." This initial effort was a forecast of what was to follow The precision of attack, cle sr enunciation and voice modulation which were characteristic features of the choir's interpretation of it were well marked in the ensuing concerted items. One of the most enchanting pieces of the evening was the melodious Welsh air " Llwyn On " (" Ash Grove ") in which the choir naay be said to have shone. There was a loud demand for an encore, and the talentld conductress again took up the baton and led her choir safely through the difficulties of the amusing piece" Dickory Dock." The individual efforts of some of the members of the choir were also very praiseworthy. The scena " l'alisererl " Trovatore) in which Miss Edith Trew took the leading part, was a dis- tinct success, and the audience showed their apprecia- tion by demanding an encore. Mention should also be made of the singing of Mies Janet Garnet, the winner of the first prize at the receat National Eisteddfod at Liverpool. She gave a very capable interpretation of the competitive solo at Liverpool " With Verdure Clad" (" Creation,") and proved herself a worthy possessor of the distinction she has gained amongst Welsh sineers. " The Swallows" was a song well suited to Miss ',Foulkes' voice, and she uttered the trills in this song as well as in the part song " Fair land we greet thee." in a highly creditable manner. Solos were also sung by Miss Mary Powell, Miss Annie Bell, Miss Annie Davies and Miss Gertrude Wedlake. and an apnreciative audience requested encores. Mr. Arthur Weber was the only male soloist of the evening and his deep bass voice was heard to advantage in "The Windmill "and "King of the Mist." Complying with an encore he sang " The Boys of the Old Brigade " which further pleased the audience. The instrumental part of the programme was capably sustained by Miss Marie Novello Williams (pianist) and Miss Backsheen Wood (violinist). Miss Williams is a pianist of great promise. She gave a brilliant performance of Liszt's " La C impanella " for which she was encored and also played the accompaniments to the choir with skill and tas'e. Miss Wood maintained the high reputation she has gained as a violinist by her performance of " Fan- tasie Brilliant" (Vieuxtempe) and " Ungarische Rhap- sodie" (Hauser). An enjoyable evening's entertainment concluded by the singing of the National Anthem in English and Welsh.

Warrington quarters, an attempt to drop a goal failing. Matters were soon reversed and a fine passing move- ment between Dickenson, Ratcliffe and Jewkes resulted in the latter scoring petween the posts, Ratcliffe adding the extra points. Passing between the three-quarters ended in Ratcliffe getting possession, but he was grassed near the line. Shortly afterwards the same player made a mark, his kick at goal being successful. Half-time arrived with the score :—Warrington, 4 goals; 6 tries (26 points) ; Wigan nil. Rain fell heavily just before the interval, and consequently the ball was very greasy, which rendered neat passing difficult. On changing ends Warrington again pressed, and a com- bined movement by the three-quarters. enabled Ratcliffe to score between the uprights,a goal resulting. Duckworth got possession of the leather and when tackled, passed in the nickof time to Allen, who scored easily. The try was not improved upon. Wigan played up desperately and over eagerness spoiled several good opportunities. Allen registered another try for Warring- ton. The whistle sounded for full time with Warrington victorioua by five goals nine tries (37 points) to nil: • Lancashire Junior League. RUNCORN RECREATION V. LATCHFORD BANGERS.—On Saturday at Runcorn. Latchford lost the toss, and on kicking off carried the ball to the Recreation's quarter. Riley, on getting the ball, scored and added a goal. After a bit of scrambline the Latchford team scored,and kicked a goal. Final:—Runcorn Recreation, ten points ; Latchford, five points. WIDNES BANGERS V. WARRINGTON RANGERS.—At Widnes on Saturday. Played in a strong wind. War- rington played five substitutes. Brett kicked off for Widnes against the wind, the homesters immediately pressing. Mather got over,snit the point was disallowed. Soon after White got over,the place failing, Mather next scored, the try being converted. White also scored. Final :—Widnes Rangere, one goat its trier ; Warring- ton Rangers, nil. RUNCORN JUNIORS V. BIRKENHEAD WANDERERS (A).— At Halton on Saturday. Birkenhead started against the wind. The Juniors here forced play. Then a knock-on by Birkenhead spoilt a good effort. The Juniors played well but were unable to do anything before half-time, when there was no scose. Baseett scored for the Juniors in the second portion,Birkenhead equalising just on time. Final :—Runcorn Juniors, one try ; Birken- head Wanderers (A), one try. THE OFFENDERS' LIST. At a meeting of the committee of this competition, held in Manchester on Tuesday night. Williams, of Barrow, was charged with tripping ; Yates, of Wigan with charging ; and Farmer, of Runcorn, with using insulting language. The charges were laid by the same referee, Mr B Ashton, of Werneth. Williams was sus- pended up to and including November 3, Yates over Saturday next, whilst Farmer was dismissed with a caution. His offence was not a serious one,and had he been suspended he could not have played against York- shire next Saturday.
